concepts.notes: Merged 3 rows (ciu:graph-representations, wikipedia:Graph_(abstract_data_type)#Common_data_structures_for_graph_representation, opendsa:Graph/GraphImpl). Open prose added in the gap inventory from dossiers/sweep-dsa.md, Candidates.

concepts.name: Whatever-first search
concepts.statement: Generic traversal: put (parent, vertex) pairs into a bag, repeatedly take one out and, if unmarked, mark it and add its neighbours; it marks exactly the vertices reachable from s, the parent edges form a spanning tree of them, and it runs in O(V + E*T) time for bag operation cost T.

concepts.name: Stack, queue and priority-queue traversals
concepts.statement: Using a stack, queue or priority queue as the bag gives depth-first search, breadth-first search and best-first search (Prim, Dijkstra, widest path); each runs in O(V+E) or O(E log E) time.

concepts.name: Breadth-first search on graphs
concepts.statement: BFS explores vertices in order of edge distance from the source using a queue, in O(V+E) with lists, and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
concepts.notes: Merged 3 rows (ciu:graph-bfs, cpa:bfs, ods:bfs).

concepts.name: BFS shortest paths in unweighted graphs
concepts.statement: BFS visits vertices in increasing distance from r and never visits unreachable ones; recording p[j] = i when j is first enqueued gives a BFS tree, and following p[j], p[p[j]], ... reconstructs a shortest path from r to j in reverse.
aliases: Breadth-first search for unweighted shortest paths
concepts.notes: Merged 3 rows (ods:bfs-shortest-paths, jeffe:bfs-shortest-paths, sdp:bfs-shortest-path). Edge to ford-relaxation dropped: Erickson frames BFS as an instance of Ford's relaxation; unweighted BFS distances need no relaxation framework, and cpa and ODS teach them from BFS alone.

concepts.name: Restoring BFS shortest paths
concepts.statement: Record each vertex's parent when it is first reached and follow parents back from the target, then reverse.

concepts.name: Applications of BFS
concepts.statement: BFS also finds connected components, least-move solutions of puzzles/games as state graphs, the shortest cycle in a directed graph, the vertices/edges on some shortest a-b path, shortest even-length walks (on a doubled state graph), and shortest paths with 0/1 weights.

concepts.name: Depth-first search on graphs
concepts.statement: DFS follows each path as deep as possible before backtracking, recursively or with an explicit stack, in O(V+E) with lists.
concepts.notes: Merged 4 rows (ciu:graph-dfs, cpa:dfs, ods:dfs, jeffe:dfs).

concepts.name: Iterative DFS with an explicit stack
concepts.statement: Replace recursion with a heap-allocated stack to avoid stack overflow on deep graphs.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (cpa:iterative-dfs, ods:dfs-iterative).

concepts.name: Implement BFS and DFS on both representations
concepts.statement: Write recursive and iterative DFS and BFS on an adjacency list and on an adjacency matrix.

concepts.name: Traversal cost restricted to the reachable part
concepts.statement: bfs and dfs from r on adjacency lists run in O(n_r + m_r) time, where n_r counts vertices reachable from r and m_r the edges whose sources are those vertices; used by several of the chapter's exercises.

concepts.name: Counting connected components
concepts.statement: Run DFS or BFS from each unvisited vertex; the number of launches is the number of components.
concepts.notes: Merged 3 rows (ciu:connected-components, cpa:connected-components, jeffe:counting-components).

concepts.name: Flood fill as a graph reduction
concepts.statement: Recolouring the connected region of a pixel image is whatever-first search on the implicit grid graph whose vertices are same-coloured pixels and edges join adjacent pixels; O(n) for n pixels.

concepts.name: Checking whether a graph is bipartite
concepts.statement: Two-colour the graph with BFS or DFS; it is bipartite exactly when no edge joins two vertices of the same colour.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (ciu:bipartite-check, cpa:bipartite-check).

concepts.name: DFS entry/exit times and ancestor test
concepts.statement: Record entry and exit times (and white/grey/black colours) during DFS; in a tree, i is an ancestor of j iff tin[i] < tin[j] and tout[i] > tout[j], checkable in O(1).
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (cpa:dfs-entry-exit-times, jeffe:pre-postorder). Source tiers differ (cpa core, jeffe stretch); reconciled to the most common, core.

concepts.name: Classification of edges by DFS
concepts.statement: Edges are tree, back, forward or cross edges according to the endpoints' colours and entry/exit times; undirected graphs have only tree and back edges.
aliases: Classifying vertices and edges in DFS
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (cpa:dfs-edge-classification, jeffe:edge-classification). Tier raised from stretch to core: it is a prerequisite of cycle-detection (core).

concepts.name: Cycle detection
concepts.statement: Detect a cycle with DFS by finding an edge back to a vertex still on the recursion stack (directed) or to a non-parent visited vertex (undirected).
aliases: Cycle detection and finding with DFS colours
concepts.notes: Merged 3 rows (ciu:cycle-detection, jeffe:cycle-detection, cpa:cycle-detection-dfs).

concepts.name: Topological order
concepts.statement: An ordering of the vertices of a directed graph in which every edge goes from an earlier to a later vertex; it exists iff the graph is acyclic and need not be unique.
aliases: Topological sort by repeatedly taking a minimal element
Topological sort as repeated selection of a minimal element
concepts.notes: Merged 3 rows (cpa:topological-order, mcs2018:10.5.1, aspnes-202:9.5.5.1). The MCS and Aspnes treatments (gap-patterns §3) prove that every finite DAG has a topological order by repeatedly taking a minimal element: Kahn's idea as an existence proof, without the data structures, so they treat this concept rather than kahn-topological-sort.

concepts.name: Topological sort
concepts.statement: A directed acyclic graph can be linearly ordered so every edge points forward, e.g. by reverse DFS finishing order, in O(V+E).
concepts.notes: Merged 3 rows (ciu:topological-sort, cpa:topological-sort, jeffe:topological-sort). Tier from CIU (required list); other sources say cpa core, jeffe stretch.

concepts.name: Kahn's algorithm
concepts.statement: Put every vertex with no incoming edge in a set S; repeatedly remove a vertex from S, append it to the order, delete its out-edges and add any vertex left with no incoming edge. If edges remain at the end the graph has a cycle; otherwise the order is topological, found in O(V+E).
aliases: Course schedule order by Kahn's algorithm
Build order by repeatedly removing independent nodes
concepts.notes: Merged 6 rows (wikipedia:Topological_sorting#Kahn's_algorithm, opendsa:Graph/GraphTopsort#Queue-based_Solution, oiwiki:graph/topo#Kahn_算法, doocs-leetcode:0207#Solution_1:_Topological_Sorting, doocs-leetcode:0210#Solution_1, icc:graphs_trees/graph_build_order). From the gap-patterns finder run (dossiers/gap-patterns.md §3). cpa says outright that it does not cover Kahn's algorithm, and Erickson and CIU teach only the DFS method, which stays the topological-sort concept beside this one.

concepts.name: Low-link values
concepts.statement: low[v] = min of tin[v], tin[p] over back edges (v,p), and low[to] over DFS-tree children; it is the earliest entry time reachable from v's subtree by one back edge.

concepts.name: Bridge (cut edge)
concepts.statement: An edge of an undirected graph whose removal increases the number of connected components.

concepts.name: Finding bridges in O(N + M)
concepts.statement: A DFS tree edge (v, to) is a bridge iff low[to] > tin[v]; skip only the edge to the parent (by edge index, to allow multi-edges).

concepts.name: Articulation point (cut vertex)
concepts.statement: A vertex whose removal, with its incident edges, increases the number of connected components of an undirected graph.

concepts.name: Articulation points in O(N + M)
concepts.statement: A non-root v is a cut vertex iff some DFS child to has low[to] >= tin[v]; the root is one iff it has more than one DFS child.

concepts.name: Strongly connected component and condensation
concepts.statement: A maximal vertex set of a directed graph with paths both ways between every pair; contracting each SCC gives the condensation graph, which is a DAG.
aliases: Strong connectivity and the strong component graph
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (cpa:scc, jeffe:strong-components). Tier raised from stretch to core: it is a prerequisite of kosaraju (core).

concepts.name: Strongly connected components (Kosaraju)
concepts.statement: Two DFS passes, one on the graph and one on its reverse in decreasing finish order, list the strongly connected components in O(V+E).
concepts.notes: Merged 3 rows (ciu:strongly-connected-components, cpa:kosaraju, jeffe:kosaraju-sharir). Tier from CIU (required list); other sources say cpa stretch, jeffe stretch.

concepts.name: Tarjan's SCC algorithm
concepts.statement: One DFS with a stack and low values; a vertex with low[v] = tin[v] is the root of an SCC, which is popped off the stack; O(n + m).
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (cpa:tarjan-scc, jeffe:tarjan-scc).

concepts.name: Building the condensation graph
concepts.statement: Map each vertex to its component's root and add an edge between roots for every edge crossing components.

concepts.name: Existence of Eulerian path/cycle
concepts.statement: A connected (ignoring isolated vertices) undirected multigraph has an Eulerian cycle iff all degrees are even, and an Eulerian path iff exactly zero or two vertices have odd degree.

concepts.name: Finding an Eulerian path in O(M)
concepts.statement: Walk unused edges from a vertex, pushing vertices on a stack and emitting each when it has no unused edges; this splices simple cycles into one Euler cycle; for a path, add an edge between the two odd vertices first and cut there.

concepts.name: Single-source shortest paths problem
concepts.statement: Given a weighted graph and source s, find the length (and a path) of the shortest path from s to every vertex.
aliases: Single-source shortest paths and shortest-path trees
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (cpa:sssp, jeffe:shortest-path-tree).

concepts.name: Edge relaxation and predecessor array
concepts.statement: Relaxing (v, to, w) sets d[to] = d[v] + w and p[to] = v when this improves d[to]; following p from the target restores a shortest path.

concepts.name: Ford's generic algorithm: relax tense edges
concepts.statement: Initialize dist(s)=0 and dist(v)=infinity; an edge u->v is tense if dist(u)+w(u->v) < dist(v); repeatedly relaxing tense edges until none remain yields correct distances and a shortest-path tree whenever there is no negative cycle.
concepts.notes: Edge to edge-relaxation added: Erickson's generic algorithm repeats the relaxation step that cpa names separately.

concepts.name: Negative edges and negative cycles
concepts.statement: With negative edge weights shortest walks may not exist (a reachable negative cycle makes distances -infinity) and shortest simple paths are NP-hard; algorithms either assume no negative cycles or report one.

concepts.name: Dijkstra's algorithm
concepts.statement: With non-negative edge weights, repeatedly settling the closest unsettled vertex and relaxing its edges gives single-source shortest paths in O((V+E) log V) with a binary heap.
concepts.notes: Merged 3 rows (ciu:dijkstra, cpa:dijkstra, jeffe:dijkstra).

concepts.name: Dijkstra with a priority queue or set
concepts.statement: On sparse graphs keep (distance, vertex) pairs in a set (erasing the old pair on improvement) or a priority queue with lazy deletion (skip entries whose distance is stale), giving O(m log n).

concepts.name: A* search
concepts.statement: Best-first search ordered by g(n)+h(n); with an admissible heuristic h it finds a shortest path, usually exploring far less than Dijkstra.

concepts.name: Bellman-Ford algorithm
concepts.statement: Relaxing every edge V-1 times gives shortest paths with negative weights allowed, in O(VE), and one more pass detects a negative cycle.
concepts.notes: Merged 3 rows (ciu:bellman-ford, cpa:bellman-ford, jeffe:bellman-ford). Tier from CIU (required list); other sources say cpa core, jeffe stretch.

concepts.name: Negative cycle detection with Bellman-Ford
concepts.statement: If some edge still relaxes in an n-th phase, a negative cycle is reachable; walking n predecessor steps back from that vertex lands on the cycle, which is then read off.

concepts.name: Shortest Path Faster Algorithm (SPFA)
concepts.statement: Queue only vertices whose distance just improved; worst case still O(nm), often much faster; counting relaxations per vertex (n) detects negative cycles.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (cpa:spfa, jeffe:moore-queue). Moore's queue-based Bellman-Ford (jeffe) is the algorithm cp-algorithms calls SPFA.

concepts.name: 0-1 BFS
concepts.statement: With edge weights 0 or 1, a deque replaces the priority queue: push to the front after a 0-edge relaxation and to the back after a 1-edge; this is Dijkstra in O(n + m).

concepts.name: Dial's algorithm
concepts.statement: With integer weights at most k, k+1 buckets of vertices indexed by distance modulo k+1 replace the priority queue.

concepts.name: D'Esopo-Pape algorithm
concepts.statement: Keep vertices in three sets (done, in deque, untouched); a vertex re-improved after being processed goes to the front of the deque, a new one to the back; usually faster than Dijkstra and Bellman-Ford but exponential in the worst case.

concepts.name: Disjoint sets (union-find)
concepts.statement: A structure over disjoint sets supporting union of two sets and find of an element's representative, stored as a forest of trees.
concepts.notes: Merged 3 rows (ciu:union-find, cpa:dsu, jeffe-notes:disjoint-set-adt). Tier set to core in the spec (sources say ciu stretch, cpa stretch, jeffe-notes stretch): kruskal (core) rests on it; ruling of 2026-11-08.

concepts.name: Shallow threaded trees
concepts.statement: Giving every element a direct pointer to its leader makes Find O(1); merging the smaller set into the larger makes Union O(log n) amortized.

concepts.name: DSU for incremental connectivity
concepts.statement: Adding edges as unions and answering 'same component?' with find_set handles an incrementally built graph in near-constant time per operation; also used for components of an image and in Kruskal.

concepts.name: Union by size / rank
concepts.statement: Attach the root of the smaller (by size or by depth bound) tree under the larger; without path compression this already bounds operations at O(log n).
aliases: Union by rank and path compression
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (cpa:dsu-union-by-rank, ciu:union-find-optimisations). ciu:union-find-optimisations also treats path-compression (row split by granularity). CIU's one row covers both heuristics; split, CIU's row treats both.

concepts.name: Path compression
concepts.statement: During find_set, re-point every visited vertex directly to the root; alone this gives O(log n) average per call.
aliases: Union by rank and path compression
concepts.notes: Merged 3 rows (cpa:dsu-path-compression, jeffe-notes:path-compression, ciu:union-find-optimisations). ciu:union-find-optimisations also treats union-by-rank (row split by granularity).

concepts.name: DSU amortised complexity is O(alpha(n))
concepts.statement: With path compression and union by size/rank, a sequence of operations costs O(alpha(n)) amortised each, alpha the inverse Ackermann function (at most 4 for practical n); stated without proof, with Fredman-Saks lower bound in the history.
aliases: The Ackermann function and its inverse
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (cpa:dsu-inverse-ackermann, jeffe-notes:inverse-ackermann). Source tiers differ (cpa stretch, jeffe-notes contest); reconciled to the most common, stretch.

concepts.name: Minimum spanning tree
concepts.statement: A spanning tree (n-1 edges connecting all vertices with no cycle) of a weighted undirected graph with least total weight.
concepts.notes: Tier raised from stretch to core: it is a prerequisite of prim (core).

concepts.name: Minimum spanning trees with distinct weights
concepts.statement: If all edge weights are distinct, a connected graph has a unique minimum spanning tree; ties can be broken consistently so this is assumed w.l.o.g.

concepts.name: Properties of minimum spanning trees
concepts.statement: An MST is unique if all weights are distinct; with positive weights it also minimises the product of weights; and it minimises the maximum edge weight among spanning trees (minimum bottleneck).

concepts.name: The only MST algorithm: safe and useless edges
concepts.statement: Maintain a forest F contained in the MST; an edge is useless if both endpoints are in one component of F and safe if it is the lightest edge leaving some component; the MST contains every safe edge and no useless edge, so adding safe edges until F spans is correct.

concepts.name: Minimum spanning tree: Prim's algorithm
concepts.statement: Grow one tree by repeatedly adding the cheapest edge leaving it; O(E log V) with a heap.
concepts.notes: Merged 3 rows (ciu:mst-prim, cpa:prim, jeffe:prim). Tier from CIU (required list); other sources say cpa stretch, jeffe core.

concepts.name: Minimum spanning tree: Kruskal's algorithm
concepts.statement: Add edges in increasing weight order, skipping any that would close a cycle (checked with union-find); O(E log E).
concepts.notes: Merged 4 rows (ciu:mst-kruskal, cpa:kruskal, cpa:kruskal-dsu, jeffe:kruskal). Tier from CIU (required list); other sources say cpa stretch, cpa stretch, jeffe core.

concepts.name: Boruvka's algorithm
concepts.statement: In each phase add all safe edges (the lightest edge leaving every component), found by one O(V+E) labeling pass; components at least halve, so it runs in O(E log V) time.

concepts.name: The backtracking pattern
concepts.statement: A backtracking algorithm builds a solution one decision at a time; each recursive call receives the remaining input and a summary of past decisions, tries every option for the next decision, and recurses.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (jeffe:backtracking-pattern, ciu:backtracking).

concepts.name: n Queens by backtracking
concepts.statement: Place queens row by row; for each row try every column that does not attack a previously placed queen and recurse, abandoning partial placements that cannot be extended.

concepts.name: Game trees and minimax
concepts.statement: A state in a two-player game with perfect information is good for the player to move iff some move leads to a state that is bad for the opponent; recursive search of the game tree decides any such game.

concepts.name: Generating all permutations by backtracking
concepts.statement: Fill positions one at a time; at each position try every unused element (tracked in a used-array), recurse, then undo the choice. n! permutations, each produced in O(n).
aliases: Permutations of a multiset by backtracking
Permutations of a string with duplicates
concepts.notes: Merged 3 rows (doocs-leetcode:0046#Solution_1:_DFS_(Backtracking), doocs-leetcode:0047#Solution_1:_Sorting_+_Backtracking, icc:recursion_dynamic/permutations). From the gap-patterns finder run (dossiers/gap-patterns.md §6). CIU's backtracking row only links to permutation and subset write-ups; no inventory row taught generation.

concepts.name: Next permutation in lexicographic order
concepts.statement: Find the largest k with a[k] < a[k+1], then the largest l > k with a[k] < a[l]; swap them and reverse a[k+1..]. Repeating from the sorted order lists all permutations lexicographically, and repeated values are handled.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (wikipedia:Permutation#Generation_in_lexicographic_order, doocs-leetcode:0031#Solution_1:_Two_traversals). From the gap-patterns finder run (dossiers/gap-patterns.md §6). Iterative, not backtracking; it sits here with the other generators.

concepts.name: Heap's algorithm
concepts.statement: Heap's algorithm generates all n! permutations, each from the previous by a single swap, by a recursion that swaps a[k-1] with a[i] or a[0] according to the parity of k; recursive and iterative forms.
concepts.notes: From the gap-patterns finder run (dossiers/gap-patterns.md §6). Tier stretch: one swap per permutation matters for contests and puzzles, not for the typical interview, where backtracking and next permutation suffice.

concepts.name: Generating all subsets
concepts.statement: Decide for each element in turn whether it is in the subset (include, recurse, exclude, recurse); the 2^n leaves of this recursion are the subsets. Equivalently, the bits of each mask 0..2^n-1 select a subset (Solution 2).
aliases: Power set: bitwise, backtracking and cascading
concepts.notes: Merged 5 rows (doocs-leetcode:0078#Solution_1:_DFS_(Backtracking), trekhleb-jsalgo:src/algorithms/sets/power-set/README.md#Algorithms, wikipedia:Power_set#Representing_subsets_as_functions, doocs-leetcode:0090#Solution_1:_Sorting_+_DFS, icc:recursion_dynamic/power_set). From the gap-patterns finder run (dossiers/gap-patterns.md §6). Kept apart from submask enumeration (7.4), which lists the submasks of one mask, and from subset sum by backtracking (17.3), which decides rather than lists.

concepts.name: Generating k-combinations by backtracking
concepts.statement: Choose elements in increasing order: either decide pick or skip for each number, or loop the next pick from i to n; stop a branch when it can no longer reach k elements.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (doocs-leetcode:0077#Solution_1:_Backtracking_(Two_Ways), doocs-leetcode:0039#Solution_1:_Sorting_+_Pruning_+_Backtracking). From the gap-patterns finder run (dossiers/gap-patterns.md §6). The lexicographic successor method is next-combination (40.5, stretch).

concepts.name: Subset sum by backtracking
concepts.statement: Whether some subset of X[1..n] sums to T is decided by recursing on whether X[n] is in the subset: SubsetSum(X[1..n-1], T) or SubsetSum(X[1..n-1], T - X[n]); O(2^n) time.

concepts.name: Text segmentation (word break) by backtracking
concepts.statement: A string A[1..n] can be split into words iff some prefix A[1..i] is a word and the suffix A[i+1..n] is splittable; the backtracking algorithm runs in exponential time in the worst case.

concepts.name: Index formulation of a recurrence
concepts.statement: Rewrite a recursive algorithm so every subproblem is identified by a few integer indices into the fixed global input (e.g. Splittable(i) for suffix A[i..n]); this exposes how many distinct subproblems exist.

concepts.name: Longest increasing subsequence by backtracking
concepts.statement: LIS can be computed by recursion either on (prev, j) - the length of the longest increasing subsequence of A[j..n] whose elements all exceed A[prev] - or on the index of the first element chosen (take 2).

concepts.name: Optimal binary search tree recurrence
concepts.statement: Given key frequencies f[1..n], the cost of an optimal BST satisfies OptCost(i,k) = sum f[i..k] + min over roots r of OptCost(i,r-1)+OptCost(r+1,k); backtracking evaluates it in exponential time.

concepts.name: Dynamic programming: overlapping subproblems
concepts.statement: A recursion whose calls repeat the same subproblems (naive Fibonacci makes O(2^n) calls) can be made polynomial by computing each of its distinct subproblems once.
aliases: Dynamic programming: reuse of overlapping subproblems
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (cpa:dp-overlapping-subproblems, ciu:dynamic-programming).

concepts.name: Memoization
concepts.statement: Store the result of each recursive subproblem the first time it is computed and look it up on later calls; for Fibonacci this turns exponential time into O(n) additions.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (jeffe:memoization, cpa:memoization).

concepts.name: Bottom-up (tabulated) DP
concepts.statement: Fill the table from the base cases upward in dependency order; when a state needs only the last few states, keep only those for O(1) memory.
aliases: Dynamic programming: filling the table deliberately
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (cpa:bottom-up-dp, jeffe:dp-fill-deliberately).

concepts.name: Dynamic programming is smart recursion
concepts.statement: Dynamic programming is recursion without repetition: specify the subproblem in English, give a recurrence, identify subproblems by indices, choose a memoization structure, find a dependency-respecting evaluation order, and analyze time and space.

concepts.name: Recognising a DP problem
concepts.statement: Spot optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems, and write the recurrence relation that defines the answer.

concepts.name: Classic DP problems
concepts.statement: Standard first DP problems: 0-1 knapsack, subset sum, longest increasing subsequence, counting grid paths, longest common subsequence, edit distance.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (cpa:classic-dp-problems, ciu:dp-classics). Tier from CIU (optional list); other sources say cpa core. cpa:classic-dp-problems also treats longest-common-subsequence (row split by granularity).

concepts.name: Fibonacci in linear time
concepts.statement: Keeping only the last two values, F_n is computed in O(n) time and O(1) memory.

concepts.name: Fibonacci via matrix exponentiation
concepts.statement: [[1,1],[1,0]]^n = [[F_{n+1},F_n],[F_n,F_{n-1}]], so F_n is computed in O(log n) by binary exponentiation of a 2x2 matrix.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (cpa:fibonacci-matrix, jeffe:fast-fibonacci).

concepts.name: Coin change: fewest coins by DP
concepts.statement: The fewest coins making value r is found by a table over coins and values: m[c][r] = min(m[c-1][r], 1 + m[c][r - coin_c]), with infinity where no change exists; the greedy method is optimal only for canonical coin systems.
aliases: Coin change as a complete knapsack
concepts.notes: Merged 4 rows (wikipedia:Change-making_problem#Simple_dynamic_programming, anfp:17.3, doocs-leetcode:0322#Solution_1:_Dynamic_Programming_(Complete_Knapsack), icc:recursion_dynamic/coin_change_min). From the gap-patterns finder run (dossiers/gap-patterns.md §7). doocs frames it as the complete knapsack (18.6); the map does not make it rest on knapsack, since Wikipedia and ANFP teach it directly.

concepts.name: Coin change: counting the ways
concepts.statement: With dp[0] = 1, for each coin and each value i from the coin upward do dp[i] += dp[i - coin]; putting the coins in the outer loop counts each combination once regardless of order. O(N·S) time, O(N) space.
aliases: number of ways to make change
Ways to make change, one array
Ways to make change, two-dimensional table
Coin change II as a complete knapsack count
concepts.notes: Merged 4 rows (algo-explanation:Dynamic_Programming/Coin_Change, icc:recursion_dynamic/coin_change_ways, icc:recursion_dynamic/coin_change, doocs-leetcode:0518#Solution_1:_Dynamic_Programming_(Complete_Knapsack)). From the gap-patterns finder run (dossiers/gap-patterns.md §7).

concepts.name: Counting grid paths
concepts.statement: The number of right/down paths to cell (i, j) is f[i][j] = f[i-1][j] + f[i][j-1] with f = 1 on the first row and column, so an m×n grid is counted in O(mn), and in O(n) memory with a rolling array; the count equals C(m+n-2, m-1).
aliases: Unique paths: backtracking, DP and Pascal's triangle
concepts.notes: Merged 4 rows (doocs-leetcode:0062#Solution_1:_Dynamic_Programming, trekhleb-jsalgo:src/algorithms/uncategorized/unique-paths/README.md#Algorithms, wikipedia:Lattice_path#Counting_lattice_paths, dmoi3:sec_counting-binom#Lattice_Paths). From the gap-patterns finder run (dossiers/gap-patterns.md §8). One concept with two derivations: the DP recurrence (doocs, trekhleb) and the binomial count (Wikipedia, Levin). cpa's classic-DP table names it only as an alias (classic-dp-problems); cpa's lattice paths avoiding obstacles (40.4) now rests on it.

concepts.name: Counting grid paths around obstacles
concepts.statement: Set f[i][j] = 0 on obstacle cells and f[i][j] = f[i-1][j] + f[i][j-1] elsewhere; borders are filled until the first obstacle. O(mn).
aliases: A robot's path around off-limits cells
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (doocs-leetcode:0063#Solution_2:_Dynamic_Programming, icc:recursion_dynamic/grid_path). From the gap-patterns finder run (dossiers/gap-patterns.md §8). Kept apart from cpa's inclusion-exclusion count with few obstacles (lattice-paths-obstacles, contest).

concepts.name: Minimum path sum in a grid
concepts.statement: f[i][j] = min(f[i-1][j], f[i][j-1]) + grid[i][j], with the first row and column as running sums; f[m-1][n-1] is the cheapest right/down path. O(mn).
concepts.notes: From the gap-patterns finder run (dossiers/gap-patterns.md §8).

concepts.name: Text segmentation by dynamic programming
concepts.statement: Memoizing Splittable(i) over i=1..n+1 and filling from n+1 down gives an O(n^2) algorithm (given constant-time IsWord).

concepts.name: Longest increasing subsequence by DP
concepts.statement: Memoizing LISbigger over all (i, j) pairs gives O(n^2) time; the 'first element' recurrence LISfirst(i) = 1 + max over j>i with A[j]>A[i] also gives O(n^2).
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (jeffe:lis-dp, cpa:lis-quadratic).

concepts.name: Restoring a DP solution with parent pointers
concepts.statement: Record for each state which predecessor achieved its optimum, then follow the pointers back from the best final state; alternatively recompute the choice to save memory.

concepts.name: LIS in O(n log n) with binary search
concepts.statement: Keep d[l] = smallest tail of an increasing subsequence of length l; d is sorted and each element updates one entry found by binary search (lower bound), giving O(n log n).

concepts.name: LIS variants: non-decreasing, counting, covering
concepts.statement: Non-decreasing needs only upper bound; the number of LIS sums ways over optimal predecessors; the minimum number of non-increasing subsequences covering a sequence equals the LIS length (duality proof).

concepts.name: Maximum subarray sum problem
concepts.statement: Find l <= r maximising a[l] + ... + a[r] for an array that may contain negative numbers.

concepts.name: Maximum subarray via prefix sums and running minimum
concepts.statement: The best sum ending at r is s[r] - min_{l<r} s[l], so one pass keeping the minimum prefix sum solves it in O(n).

concepts.name: Kadane's algorithm
concepts.statement: Accumulate a running sum, reset it to 0 whenever it becomes negative, and track the maximum value seen; O(n) time and O(1) space.

concepts.name: Maximum-sum submatrix
concepts.statement: Fixing a pair of rows and running Kadane on the column sums gives O(n^3).

concepts.name: Maximum-average subarray with a length bound
concepts.statement: Binary search on the average x, subtracting x from every element and checking for a subarray of length at least L with non-negative sum.

concepts.name: Subset sum by DP (pseudo-polynomial)
concepts.statement: Memoizing SS(i, t) for 1<=i<=n, 0<=t<=T solves subset sum in O(nT) time, which is not polynomial in the input size.

concepts.name: 0-1 knapsack
concepts.statement: With f[i][j] the best value from the first i items within capacity j, f[i][j] = max(f[i-1][j], f[i-1][j-w_i] + v_i), solvable in O(nW).

concepts.name: One-dimensional knapsack and iteration order
concepts.statement: Drop the item dimension: iterate capacity downward for 0-1 knapsack (each item once) and upward for complete knapsack (unbounded reuse); the same update with the wrong order solves the other problem.

concepts.name: Complete (unbounded) knapsack
concepts.statement: With unlimited copies, f[i][j] = max(f[i-1][j], f[i][j-w_i] + v_i), O(nW).

concepts.name: Bounded knapsack by binary grouping
concepts.statement: Split k_i copies into bundles of 1, 2, 4, ... plus a remainder so every count up to k_i is a sum of bundles; the bounded problem becomes 0-1 knapsack in O(W sum log k_i).

concepts.name: Bounded knapsack by monotone queue
concepts.statement: Group capacities by residue mod w_i; each transition becomes a sliding-window maximum, giving O(nW).

concepts.name: Edit distance
concepts.statement: The minimum number of insertions, deletions and substitutions turning A[1..m] into B[1..n] satisfies Edit(i,j) = min(Edit(i-1,j)+1, Edit(i,j-1)+1, Edit(i-1,j-1)+[A[i]!=B[j]]), computable in O(mn) time.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (jeffe:edit-distance, ciu:edit-distance).

concepts.name: Longest common subsequence
concepts.statement: The longest common subsequence of strings a and b satisfies L[i][j] = L[i-1][j-1] + 1 when a_i = b_j and max(L[i-1][j], L[i][j-1]) otherwise, so a table over prefix pairs gives it in O(nm) time.
concepts.notes: cpa:classic-dp-problems also treats classic-dp-problems (row split by granularity). Bridge concept split out of cpa's classic-DP table, which names LCS (alias) but has no article; the statement is the map's own. Prose gap: no open source teaches LCS as a section (jeffe-notes D-faster-dynprog mentions it, NC).

concepts.name: RNA secondary structure
concepts.statement: A worked interval DP example from the Coursera course: maximise base pairings over substrings, with running time analysed.

concepts.name: Dynamic programming on trees
concepts.statement: On a rooted tree, a maximum independent set can be computed by recursing over children, memoizing one value (or two: with/without v) per node and filling in postorder, in O(n) time.
aliases: maximum independent set in a tree

concepts.name: Optimal binary search trees by DP
concepts.statement: Filling OptCost(i,k) by increasing interval length k-i computes an optimal BST in O(n^3) time.

concepts.name: Memoization and dynamic programming in dags
concepts.statement: Any recurrence's subproblems form a dependency dag; memoized recursion is a depth-first search of that dag and a valid evaluation order is a reverse topological order (e.g. longest path in a dag in O(V+E)).

concepts.name: Shortest paths in dags
concepts.statement: Relaxing the out-edges of vertices in topological order computes shortest (or longest) paths in a dag in O(V+E) time, even with negative weights; it is dynamic programming over the dag.

concepts.name: All-pairs shortest paths
concepts.statement: Compute dist(u,v) and pred(u,v) for every pair of vertices; output size is Theta(V^2).
concepts.notes: Tier raised from stretch to core: it is a prerequisite of floyd-warshall (core).

concepts.name: APSP by repeated single-source
concepts.statement: Running BFS, Dijkstra or Bellman-Ford from every vertex gives APSP in O(VE), O(VE log V) or O(V^2 E) time respectively.

concepts.name: Reweighting with vertex potentials
concepts.statement: Replacing w(u->v) by w(u->v) + pi(u) - pi(v) changes every u-to-v path length by the same amount pi(u)-pi(v), so shortest paths are preserved; with pi = distances from a new source all new weights are non-negative.

concepts.name: Johnson's algorithm
concepts.statement: Add a source joined to all vertices by zero-weight edges, run Bellman-Ford to get potentials, reweight, then run Dijkstra from every vertex: O(VE log V) APSP with negative edges.

concepts.name: Floyd-Warshall algorithm
concepts.statement: Before phase k, d[i][j] is the shortest i->j path using only intermediate vertices < k; d[i][j] = min(d[i][j], d[i][k] + d[k][j]) over k, i, j yields all-pairs distances in O(n^3) when no negative cycles exist.
concepts.notes: Merged 3 rows (cpa:floyd-warshall, jeffe:floyd-warshall, ciu:apsp-dp). Tier set to core in the spec (sources say cpa core, jeffe stretch, ciu stretch): floyd-warshall-path (core) rests on it. ciu:apsp-dp also treats apsp-dp (row split by granularity). CIU's APSP-by-DP row names Floyd-Warshall and matrix-style DPs; it treats both floyd-warshall and apsp-dp.

concepts.name: Restoring Floyd-Warshall paths
concepts.statement: Store the phase k that last improved d[i][j] and recurse on (i, k) and (k, j).

concepts.name: Floyd-Warshall with negative cycles
concepts.statement: After running, d[t][t] < 0 marks t on a negative cycle; any pair (i, j) with d[i][t] < INF and d[t][j] < INF for such t has no shortest path (minus infinity).

concepts.name: Finding any negative cycle
concepts.statement: Initialise all d to 0 (a virtual source to every vertex) and run Bellman-Ford n phases; a vertex relaxed in the last phase leads back to a negative cycle; Floyd-Warshall's negative diagonal finds all pairs without a shortest path.

concepts.name: APSP by dynamic programming on path length
concepts.statement: dist(u,v,l) = min over edges x->v of dist(u,x,l-1) + w(x->v) gives an O(V^4) algorithm; halving/doubling the edge bound gives O(V^3 log V).
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (jeffe:apsp-dp, ciu:apsp-dp). Tier from CIU (optional list); other sources say jeffe contest. ciu:apsp-dp also treats floyd-warshall (row split by granularity).

concepts.name: Counting paths of fixed length by matrix power
concepts.statement: The (i, j) entry of the k-th power of the adjacency matrix counts walks of exactly k edges from i to j; binary exponentiation gives O(n^3 log k).
aliases: Counting paths of length k by adjacency-matrix power
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (cpa:paths-fixed-length-count, cpa:paths-length-k-matrix). Source tiers differ (cpa contest, cpa stretch); reconciled to the most common, stretch. cpa teaches this twice (graph/fixed_length_paths and algebra/binary-exp#counting paths); joined. Assumes, untaught in the map: matrix multiplication.

concepts.name: Funny (min-plus) matrix multiplication
concepts.statement: The O(V^3 log V) APSP algorithm is repeated squaring of the weight matrix under the (min,+) semiring.
aliases: Shortest paths of fixed length by min-plus product
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (jeffe:min-plus-product, cpa:min-plus-matrix-power).

concepts.name: Warning: greed is stupid
concepts.statement: Greedy choices usually give wrong answers for optimization problems (shown with a greedy counterexample); a greedy algorithm needs a proof, so the default is to try recursion/DP first.

concepts.name: Greedy correctness by exchange argument
concepts.statement: To prove a greedy algorithm optimal, take an optimal solution that differs from the greedy choice, swap in the greedy choice without making it worse, and conclude by induction that greedy is optimal.

concepts.name: Storing files on tape
concepts.statement: To minimize the expected cost of accessing files stored sequentially, sort them by length (or by length/frequency ratio when access frequencies differ); proved by an exchange argument.

concepts.name: Class (interval) scheduling: earliest finish first
concepts.statement: Repeatedly choosing the compatible class that ends first yields a maximum set of non-overlapping intervals in O(n log n) time.
aliases: Unweighted interval scheduling: earliest finish first
Activity selection: greedy by finish time
Fewest intervals to remove for no overlap
concepts.notes: Merged 6 rows (jeffe:interval-scheduling, wikipedia:Interval_scheduling#Unweighted, wikipedia:Activity_selection_problem#Algorithm, anfp:17.2, anfp:18.3, doocs-leetcode:0435#Solution_1:_Sorting_+_Greedy). The map already had it from Erickson 4.2; the gap-patterns run (§5) added the Wikipedia, ANFP and doocs treatments.

concepts.name: Stable matching (Gale-Shapley)
concepts.statement: If unmatched proposers repeatedly propose to their most preferred not-yet-proposed partner and receivers keep the best offer so far, the algorithm halts after O(n^2) proposals with a stable matching that is best for every proposer.

concepts.name: Merging overlapping intervals
concepts.statement: Sort intervals by start; scan them, extending the current merged interval while the next one starts no later than its end, and starting a new one otherwise. O(n log n).
aliases: Inserting an interval into sorted disjoint intervals
concepts.notes: Merged 3 rows (doocs-leetcode:0056#Solution_1:_Sorting_+_One-pass_Traversal, doocs-leetcode:0057#Solution_2:_One-pass_Traversal, doocs-leetcode:0252#Solution_1:_Sorting). From the gap-patterns finder run (dossiers/gap-patterns.md §5). Open prose at problem level only (doocs). Sits with interval scheduling, after sorting.

concepts.name: Interval partitioning: minimum rooms as maximum overlap
concepts.statement: Add +1 at each meeting's start and -1 at its end in a difference array over time; the largest prefix sum is the largest number of meetings in progress at once, which is the minimum number of rooms.
aliases: Minimum meeting rooms as maximum overlap
concepts.notes: From the gap-patterns finder run (dossiers/gap-patterns.md §5). Also the sweep line over intervals: +1 at each start and -1 at each end, read in time order. cpa's union of segments (44.3) is the same sweep for lengths and stays there. Its only open prose is the doocs write-up; Erickson's interval-colouring exercise (ch. 4, unkeyed) is an exercise, not prose.

concepts.name: Prefix-free codes as binary trees
concepts.statement: A binary code is prefix-free if no codeword is a prefix of another; such codes are exactly binary trees with symbols at leaves, and the encoded length is the sum of f[i]*depth(i).

concepts.name: Huffman codes
concepts.statement: Repeatedly merging the two least frequent symbols into a new symbol builds an optimal prefix-free code; O(n log n) with a priority queue.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (jeffe:huffman, ciu:huffman). Edge to compression dropped: CIU files Huffman under Compression; the greedy construction needs prefix codes and a priority queue, not the compression chapter.

concepts.name: Maximum number of jobs meeting deadlines
concepts.statement: Process deadlines in decreasing order, push each job into a priority queue keyed by duration, and fill each gap down to the next deadline with the shortest remaining jobs, running the last one partially and returning its remainder to the queue; O(n log n).

concepts.name: Matroids and the greedy algorithm
concepts.statement: A matroid is a ground set with a non-empty family of independent sets closed under subsets and satisfying the exchange property; for every weight function the greedy algorithm finds a maximum-weight basis exactly when the structure is a matroid.

concepts.name: Scheduling unit jobs with deadlines
concepts.statement: Sets of unit-time jobs that can all meet their deadlines form a matroid, so greedily taking jobs in decreasing profit order while feasible maximizes total profit.

concepts.name: Single-machine scheduling with linear penalties
concepts.statement: Swapping adjacent jobs shows that with penalties c_i t the optimal order sorts jobs by t_i / c_i (Smith's rule).

concepts.name: Exponential and identical penalty cases
concepts.statement: With c_i e^(alpha t) sort by (1 - e^(alpha t_i))/c_i; with one shared increasing penalty sort by processing time.

concepts.name: Livshits-Kladov theorem
concepts.statement: The adjacent-exchange permutation method works only for linear, exponential and identical-monotone penalty functions.

concepts.name: Johnson's rule for two-machine flow shop
concepts.statement: To minimise makespan when every job runs on machine 1 then machine 2, put jobs with a_i <= b_i first in increasing a_i, then the rest in decreasing b_i: O(n log n).

concepts.name: Brute-force substring search
concepts.statement: Try every alignment of the pattern against the text; O(mn) worst case.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (ciu:substring-search-brute-force, jeffe-notes:brute-force-matching).

concepts.name: Boyer-Moore (and Horspool)
concepts.statement: Compare the pattern right to left and skip ahead using bad-character (and good-suffix) rules; sublinear on typical text.

concepts.name: Polynomial rolling hash of a string
concepts.statement: hash(s) = sum s[i] p^i mod m, with p a prime near the alphabet size (e.g. 31) and m a large prime (e.g. 1e9+9); equal strings have equal hashes and unequal ones collide with probability about 1/m.
aliases: Polynomial hashing for arrays and strings
concepts.notes: Merged 3 rows (cpa:polynomial-hash, ods:polynomial-hash, ciu:rolling-hash). Tier set to core in the spec (sources say cpa stretch, ods stretch, ciu stretch): prefix-hash-substring and rabin-karp (core) rest on it. ODS's polynomial hash, cpa's polynomial rolling hash and CIU's rolling hash are one concept. Assumes, untaught in the map: modular arithmetic.

concepts.name: Substring hash from prefix hashes
concepts.statement: With prefix hashes, hash(s[i..j]) * p^i = H[j+1] - H[i]; compare two substrings by multiplying both to a common power (or using a modular inverse) in O(1).
concepts.notes: Tier raised from stretch to core: it is a prerequisite of rabin-karp (core).

concepts.name: Grouping duplicate strings by hash
concepts.statement: Hash every string, sort hashes with indices, and group equal hashes, finding duplicates in O(nm + n log n) instead of O(nm log n).

concepts.name: Collision probability and double hashing
concepts.statement: Comparing one string against many raises collision odds roughly to (number of comparisons)/m by the birthday effect; using two independent moduli (or one 64-bit modulus) makes collisions negligible.
concepts.notes: Assumes, untaught in the map: birthday paradox.

concepts.name: Counting distinct substrings by hashing
concepts.statement: For each length l, collect the normalised hashes of all length-l substrings and count distinct values; O(n^2 log n).

concepts.name: Rabin-Karp
concepts.statement: Compare a rolling hash of each text window with the pattern's hash and verify on a match; expected O(n+m).
concepts.notes: Merged 3 rows (ciu:rabin-karp, cpa:rabin-karp, jeffe-notes:karp-rabin). Tier from CIU (required list); other sources say cpa stretch, jeffe-notes stretch.

concepts.name: String matching with a finite-state machine
concepts.statement: Redundant comparisons can be avoided by a finite-state machine whose state is the length of the longest pattern prefix that is a suffix of the text read so far; with failure links this is the Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm, running in O(n) after preprocessing.
concepts.notes: Tier raised from stretch to core: it is a prerequisite of prefix-function-linear (core).

concepts.name: Prefix function
concepts.statement: pi[i] is the length of the longest proper prefix of s[0..i] that is also a suffix of it; pi[0] = 0.
concepts.notes: Tier raised from stretch to core: it is a prerequisite of prefix-function-linear (core).

concepts.name: Computing the prefix function in O(n)
concepts.statement: Since pi[i+1] <= pi[i] + 1, and on a mismatch the next candidate length is pi[j-1], following these links computes the whole array in O(n) amortised, online.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (cpa:prefix-function-linear, jeffe-notes:failure-function). Tier raised from stretch to core: it is a prerequisite of kmp (core).

concepts.name: Knuth-Morris-Pratt
concepts.statement: Precompute, for each pattern prefix, the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix, so the text pointer never moves back; O(n+m).
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (ciu:kmp, cpa:kmp). Tier from CIU (required list); other sources say cpa stretch.

concepts.name: Shortest period / string compression
concepts.statement: With k = n - pi[n-1], if k divides n then s is a repetition of its prefix of length k (the shortest such); otherwise no compression exists. The Z-function gives the same answer.

concepts.name: Counting occurrences of each prefix
concepts.statement: Count how often each prefix occurs by tallying pi values and propagating counts along pi links from long to short.

concepts.name: KMP automaton
concepts.statement: Precompute transitions (state = current pi value, next character) for s + # so the text is processed with O(1) per character without storing it; built in O(n k).
concepts.notes: Assumes, untaught in the map: finite automaton.

concepts.name: Counting distinct substrings incrementally
concepts.statement: When appending c to s, the new substrings are the suffixes of s+c longer than the maximum prefix function (or Z) value of reverse(s+c); summing gives O(n^2) overall.

concepts.name: Z-function
concepts.statement: z[i] is the length of the longest common prefix of s and the suffix s[i..]; z[0] is taken as 0.

concepts.name: Computing the Z-function in O(n)
concepts.statement: Maintain the rightmost match segment [l, r); for i < r start from min(r - i, z[i - l]) and extend naively; every extension step moves r right, so the total is O(n).

concepts.name: Pattern search with the Z-function
concepts.statement: Compute Z of p + separator + t; positions in the t part with z = |p| are occurrences, in O(|p| + |t|).

concepts.name: Suffix array
concepts.statement: The sorted array of all suffixes of a string, supporting substring search by binary search and many string queries.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (ciu:suffix-array, cpa:suffix-array). Tier from CIU (required list); other sources say cpa stretch.

concepts.name: Suffix array by prefix doubling in O(n log n)
concepts.statement: Sort cyclic shifts of s + $ by their first 2^k characters, using equivalence classes from round k and counting sort on pairs, for log n rounds; this yields the suffix array.

concepts.name: Substring search and comparison with a suffix array
concepts.statement: Binary search the suffix array for a pattern in O(|p| log |t|); keeping the doubling rounds' class arrays compares any two substrings in O(1) and gives LCP in O(log n).

concepts.name: Common distributions: uniform, Bernoulli, binomial, geometric
concepts.statement: The notes define the uniform, Bernoulli, binomial and geometric distributions with their expectations, e.g. a geometric variable with success probability p has expectation 1/p.

concepts.name: Removing bias from coin flips
concepts.statement: Flip a biased coin twice: output heads on HT, tails on TH, and retry on HH or TT; this yields a fair bit in 1/(p(1-p)) expected pairs (von Neumann), and a fair coin can simulate any known bias.

concepts.name: Coupon collecting (Pokemon collecting)
concepts.statement: Collecting all n equally likely types takes n*H_n = Theta(n log n) expected trials; after n trials the expected number of distinct types seen is about (1-1/e)n.

concepts.name: Deterministic vs. randomized algorithms; expected running time
concepts.statement: A randomized algorithm's running time is a random variable; we bound its expectation for the worst-case input, separating Las Vegas algorithms (always correct) from Monte Carlo ones (probably correct).
concepts.notes: Edge to random-variable added: its running time is a random variable whose expectation is bounded (ruling 18).

concepts.name: Generating random permutations (shuffling)
concepts.statement: Swapping each A[i] with a uniformly random element of A[1..i] (Fisher-Yates) produces every permutation with probability 1/n!, in O(n) time; plausible-looking variants are biased.

concepts.name: Markov's inequality
concepts.statement: For a non-negative random variable X and z > 0, Pr[X >= z] <= E[X]/z.

concepts.name: Chebyshev's inequality
concepts.statement: Pr[|X - E[X]| >= z] <= Var[X]/z^2; for sums of pairwise independent indicators the variance is at most the mean.

concepts.name: Chernoff bounds
concepts.statement: For a sum X of independent indicator variables with mean mu, Pr[X >= (1+d)mu] <= (e^d/(1+d)^(1+d))^mu, and similar lower-tail bounds; deviations shrink exponentially in mu.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (jeffe-notes:chernoff-bound, ciu:large-deviations). Tier from CIU (optional list); other sources say jeffe-notes contest.

concepts.name: Treap depth with high probability
concepts.statement: Chernoff bounds show every node of a treap with random priorities has depth O(log n) with high probability, not just in expectation.

concepts.name: Markov chains
concepts.statement: A random process whose next state depends only on the current one, described by transition probabilities.

concepts.name: Random walks
concepts.statement: A walk that moves randomly at each step, e.g. gambler's ruin; hitting probabilities and times follow from recurrences.

concepts.name: Markov text generation
concepts.statement: Generate text by sampling each word from the words observed to follow the previous one.

concepts.name: Finding the maximum needs n-1 comparisons
concepts.statement: Every element other than the maximum must lose at least one comparison, so any algorithm needs n-1 comparisons; an adversary argument makes this precise.

concepts.name: Adversary arguments
concepts.statement: To prove a lower bound, imagine an adversary that answers queries consistently but so as to keep the answer undetermined as long as possible (three-card and n-card monte).

concepts.name: Finding the minimum and maximum: ceil(3n/2) - 2
concepts.statement: Pairing elements and comparing winners and losers finds both min and max in ceil(3n/2) - 2 comparisons, and an adversary argument shows this is optimal.

concepts.name: Evasive graph properties
concepts.statement: A graph property is evasive if every algorithm must query all n(n-1)/2 edge slots in the worst case; connectedness is evasive by an adversary that answers 'no edge' unless that would disconnect the graph.

concepts.name: Circuit satisfiability
concepts.statement: CircuitSAT asks whether a boolean circuit of AND, OR and NOT gates has an input assignment making its output true; no polynomial-time algorithm is known.

concepts.name: P, NP and NP-completeness
concepts.statement: P is the class of problems solvable in polynomial time; NP those whose solutions can be checked in polynomial time; NP-complete problems are the hardest in NP.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (ciu:p-np, jeffe:p-np). Tier from CIU (required list); other sources say jeffe stretch.

concepts.name: NP-hard, NP-easy and NP-complete
concepts.statement: A problem is NP-hard if a polynomial-time algorithm for it would give one for every NP problem, NP-easy if it is solvable in polynomial time given an NP oracle, and NP-complete if it is NP-hard and in NP.
concepts.notes: Tier raised from stretch to core: it is a prerequisite of approximation-algorithms (core).

concepts.name: Cook-Levin: SAT is NP-hard
concepts.statement: CircuitSAT (and hence SAT) is NP-hard; to prove a problem X NP-hard, reduce a known NP-hard problem to X in polynomial time (CircuitSAT reduces to SAT via one variable and clause set per gate).

concepts.name: Beyond NP: PSPACE, EXP and decidability
concepts.statement: P and NP are the start of a hierarchy: PSPACE (canonical QBF), EXP, NEXP, EXPSPACE, and undecidable problems such as halting; many games are PSPACE- or EXP-hard.

concepts.name: Polynomial-time reductions
concepts.statement: Showing problem A reduces to B in polynomial time transfers hardness from A to B; this is how NP-completeness is proved.

concepts.name: The NP-hardness proof pattern
concepts.statement: To prove X NP-hard: pick a known NP-hard problem Y, describe a polynomial-time transformation of Y-instances to X-instances, and prove both directions (good Y instance -> good X instance and conversely).

concepts.name: 3SAT is NP-hard
concepts.statement: CircuitSAT reduces to 3SAT by rewriting each gate as at most three-literal clauses; so satisfiability of 3CNF formulas is NP-hard.

concepts.name: Maximum independent set is NP-hard
concepts.statement: From a 3CNF formula with k clauses build a graph with a triangle per clause and edges between complementary literals; it has an independent set of size k iff the formula is satisfiable.

concepts.name: Clique and vertex cover are NP-hard
concepts.statement: S is independent in G iff S is a clique in the complement of G iff V\S is a vertex cover of G, so MaxClique and MinVertexCover are NP-hard by easy reductions from MaxIndSet.

concepts.name: Graph 3-colouring is NP-hard
concepts.statement: A reduction from 3SAT using a truth triangle and clause gadgets shows 3Colour, and hence chromatic number, is NP-hard; 2-colouring is solvable in linear time.

concepts.name: Hamiltonian cycle (and TSP) is NP-hard
concepts.statement: Hamiltonian cycle in directed graphs is NP-hard by a reduction from vertex cover (or 3SAT) with gadgets per edge; undirected Hamiltonian cycle and the traveling salesman problem follow.

concepts.name: Subset sum is NP-hard
concepts.statement: Encoding a vertex cover instance as base-4 numbers shows subset sum is NP-hard; this does not contradict the O(nT) algorithm because T can be exponential in the input size (weak NP-hardness).

concepts.name: Recognising NP-complete problems in disguise
concepts.statement: Identify famous NP-complete problems such as travelling salesman, knapsack and satisfiability when an interview question restates them.
concepts.notes: Kept apart from Erickson's catalog (np-hard-catalog): recognising a famous problem in disguise needs P and NP, not the reduction machinery the catalog rests on.

concepts.name: A catalog of NP-hard problems
concepts.statement: Useful NP-hard starting points include planar CircuitSAT, 1-in-3 SAT, Not-All-Equal SAT, planar SAT, exact cover by 3-sets, partition, 3-partition, set cover, hitting set, longest path, Steiner tree, MaxSAT and MaxCut, plus puzzles such as Minesweeper and Sudoku.

concepts.name: Choosing the right problem to reduce from
concepts.statement: Pick a source problem structurally close to the target: SAT variants for constraint/choice problems, independent set/vertex cover/clique for graph selection, Hamiltonian cycle for ordering, subset sum/partition for numbers.

concepts.name: A frivolous example: international draughts
concepts.statement: On an n x n board, international draughts' forced-maximum-capture rule makes merely finding a legal move NP-hard, by Hearn's reduction from Hamiltonian cycle with vertex and arc gadgets.

concepts.name: Approximation algorithms and ratios
concepts.statement: An algorithm is an alpha-approximation if on every instance its output is within a factor alpha of the optimum (A(X) <= alpha OPT(X) for minimization); proofs compare against a lower bound on OPT.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (jeffe-notes:approximation-ratio, ciu:approximation-algorithms). Tier from CIU (required list); other sources say jeffe-notes stretch.

concepts.name: Greedy load balancing
concepts.statement: Assigning each job to the currently least-loaded machine gives makespan at most 2 OPT; sorting jobs in decreasing order first improves this to 3/2 OPT (and in fact 4/3 - 1/(3m)).

concepts.name: Vertex cover approximation
concepts.statement: Greedily taking a vertex of maximum degree is an O(log n)-approximation; the 'obviously stupid' rule of taking both endpoints of any remaining edge is a 2-approximation, essentially the best known, and extends to hitting set.

concepts.name: Greedy set cover and hitting set
concepts.statement: Repeatedly choosing the set that covers the most uncovered elements is an H_n = O(log n) approximation for set cover (and for hitting set).

concepts.name: Traveling salesman: hardness and metric approximation
concepts.statement: General TSP has no polynomial-time approximation within any factor unless P=NP, but for metric TSP doubling an MST and shortcutting gives a 2-approximation (Christofides improves to 3/2).

concepts.name: k-center clustering
concepts.statement: Gonzalez's algorithm picks each next center as the point farthest from the current centers, giving a 2-approximation; doing better than 2 is NP-hard.

concepts.name: An FPTAS for subset sum
concepts.statement: Trimming the list of reachable sums so that no two kept values are within a factor (1 + eps/2n) gives a (1 - eps)-approximation in time polynomial in n and 1/eps.

concepts.name: Fixed-parameter algorithms
concepts.statement: Some NP-hard problems are fast when a chosen parameter k is small, running in f(k)*poly(n).

concepts.name: Faster exponential algorithms for 3SAT
concepts.statement: Branching on the literals of a short clause (with simplification) solves 3SAT in O(c^n poly(n)) time for c < 2, e.g. a recurrence like T(n) <= T(n-1)+T(n-2)+T(n-3) gives about 1.84^n.

concepts.name: Faster exponential algorithms for maximum independent set
concepts.statement: Branching on a vertex of high degree (exclude it, or include it and delete its neighbours), with simple rules for low-degree vertices, gives MIS in O(c^n) time for c well below 2.

concepts.name: CPU components: ALU, registers and RAM
concepts.statement: The ALU does arithmetic and logic, registers hold the operands in use, and RAM holds program and data addressed by the CPU.

concepts.name: How a CPU executes a program
concepts.statement: The CPU repeatedly fetches an instruction from memory, decodes it and executes it, advancing the program counter.

concepts.name: Memory hierarchy and CPU caches
concepts.statement: Small fast caches between registers and RAM exploit temporal and spatial locality; misses, lines and associativity determine performance.

concepts.name: Building a computer from logic gates
concepts.statement: From NAND gates up through an ALU, CPU, assembler and compiler (NAND to Tetris).

concepts.name: How a compiler works
concepts.statement: A compiler lexes, parses, analyses and generates code for a program, translating source to machine code.

concepts.name: Compiler optimisation
concepts.statement: Compilers transform code (inlining, constant folding, loop optimisations) to run faster without changing behaviour.

concepts.name: Garbage collection
concepts.statement: Automatic reclamation of unreachable memory, e.g. CPython's reference counting plus a cycle-detecting generational collector, and the JVM's collectors.

concepts.name: Processes versus threads
concepts.statement: A process has its own address space (code, static data, heap, stack, file descriptors); threads in one process share all of it except each thread's stack, registers and program counter.

concepts.name: Interrupts and context switching
concepts.statement: Interrupts let the OS take the CPU; a context switch saves one thread's registers and state and restores another's.

concepts.name: Paging, segmentation and virtual memory
concepts.statement: Each process sees its own virtual address space, mapped to physical memory in pages by the OS and hardware.

concepts.name: Fork and copy-on-write
concepts.statement: A forked child shares the parent's pages read-only and copies a page only when one of them writes to it.

concepts.name: Locks, mutexes, semaphores and monitors
concepts.statement: Primitives that serialise access to shared state: a mutex admits one holder, a semaphore a counted number, a monitor bundles a lock with condition waiting.

concepts.name: Deadlock and livelock
concepts.statement: Deadlock: threads wait forever on each other's resources; livelock: threads keep reacting to each other without progress.

concepts.name: Concurrency in Python and the GIL
concepts.statement: CPython's global interpreter lock lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time, so threads help I/O-bound work; asyncio and processes are the alternatives.

concepts.name: Parallel programming
concepts.statement: Splitting work across cores (task and data parallelism) and reasoning about its speed-up.

concepts.name: OSI and TCP/IP models
concepts.statement: Network functions are split into layers (link, internet, transport, application) and packets are routed hop by hop across the internet.

concepts.name: Subnetting and CIDR notation
concepts.statement: An IP prefix a.b.c.d/n names the network whose addresses share the first n bits.

concepts.name: TCP
concepts.statement: TCP is a connection-oriented protocol over IP: handshakes open and close connections, and sequence numbers, checksums, acknowledgements and retransmission deliver packets in order and uncorrupted, with flow and congestion control; the guarantees cost delay. Use it when all data must arrive intact (web servers, databases, SMTP, FTP, SSH).

concepts.name: UDP
concepts.statement: UDP is connectionless: datagrams may arrive out of order or not at all and there is no congestion control, so it is more efficient; it can broadcast (as DHCP needs). Use it when you need the lowest latency, late data is worse than lost data, or you implement your own error correction (VoIP, video chat, streaming, realtime games).

concepts.name: TCP versus UDP
concepts.statement: TCP gives reliable, ordered, connection-based byte streams with flow and congestion control; UDP sends independent datagrams with no guarantees and less overhead.

concepts.name: Connection pooling
concepts.statement: Many open TCP connections, e.g. between web server threads and memcached, cost memory; connection pooling, or UDP where applicable, helps. The web crawler keeps many connections open through a pool to raise throughput and cut memory.
concepts.notes: Tier raised from stretch to core: it is a prerequisite of crawler-throughput (core).

concepts.name: Socket programming
concepts.statement: Open, bind, connect, send and receive over TCP or UDP sockets.

concepts.name: HTTP
concepts.statement: HTTP is a request/response protocol for encoding and transporting data between client and server; a request is a verb plus a resource, and being self-contained it can pass through routers and servers that load balance, cache, encrypt and compress. It is an application-layer protocol over TCP and UDP.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (sdp:http, ciu:http).

concepts.name: HTTP verbs: idempotent, safe, cacheable
concepts.statement: GET reads a resource (idempotent, safe, cacheable); POST creates a resource or triggers processing (not idempotent, not safe, cacheable only with freshness info); PUT creates or replaces (idempotent); PATCH partially updates (not idempotent); DELETE deletes (idempotent). Idempotent means repeatable without different outcomes.

concepts.name: TLS and HTTPS
concepts.statement: TLS authenticates the server with certificates and encrypts the connection; HTTPS is HTTP over TLS.

concepts.name: Serialisation formats
concepts.statement: Thrift, Protocol Buffers, Avro and MessagePack encode structured data compactly with a schema.
concepts.notes: Tier set to core in the spec (sources say ciu stretch): rpc (core) rests on it.

concepts.name: Remote procedure call (RPC)
concepts.statement: In an RPC a client runs a procedure in another address space as if it were local: the client stub marshals the procedure id and arguments, OS communication modules carry the message, and the server stub unmarshals it and calls the procedure. RPC exposes behaviours and is often used internally for performance (Protobuf, Thrift, Avro); it couples clients to the implementation, needs a new API per operation, is hard to debug and fits HTTP caches poorly.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (sdp:rpc, ciu:rpc). Tier set to core in the spec (sources say sdp core, ciu stretch): rpc-vs-rest (core) rests on it.

concepts.name: REST
concepts.statement: REST is a stateless, cacheable client/server style where clients act on resources the server manages: identify resources by URI, change them through HTTP verbs, headers and body, report errors with status codes, and be browsable (HATEOAS). It exposes data, minimises coupling, suits public APIs and horizontal scaling; it fits non-hierarchical queries and actions poorly, needs several round trips for nested resources, and payloads bloat over time.

concepts.name: RPC vs REST
concepts.statement: The same operations as RPC use action endpoints (POST /signup, GET /readPerson?personid=1234, POST /removeItem) and as REST use resources and verbs (POST /persons, GET /persons/1234, DELETE /items/456); public APIs tend to be REST, internal communication RPC.

concepts.name: HATEOAS
concepts.statement: Hypermedia as the engine of application state: a RESTful web service should be fully accessible in a browser.

concepts.name: Unit testing
concepts.statement: Tests that check one unit of code in isolation against expected results.

concepts.name: Mock objects
concepts.statement: Stand-in objects that imitate a dependency and record how they are used, so a unit can be tested alone.

concepts.name: Integration testing
concepts.statement: Tests that check several units or services working together.

concepts.name: Dependency injection
concepts.statement: Pass a component its dependencies instead of having it build them, so tests can substitute fakes.

concepts.name: Test-driven development
concepts.statement: Write a failing test first, then the code to pass it, then refactor.

concepts.name: UML class diagrams
concepts.statement: Read and sketch basic UML diagrams of classes and their relationships.

concepts.name: Creational design patterns
concepts.statement: Singleton, factory and abstract factory, and prototype control how objects are created.
concepts.notes: Assumes, untaught in the map: object-oriented programming.

concepts.name: Structural design patterns
concepts.statement: Adapter, decorator, facade, proxy, composite and flyweight compose classes and objects into larger structures.
concepts.notes: Assumes, untaught in the map: object-oriented programming.

concepts.name: Behavioural design patterns
concepts.statement: Strategy, observer, visitor, command, state, memento, iterator and delegate assign responsibilities and communication between objects.
concepts.notes: Assumes, untaught in the map: object-oriented programming.

concepts.name: Single responsibility principle
concepts.statement: A class should have one reason to change.
concepts.notes: Assumes, untaught in the map: object-oriented programming.

concepts.name: Open/closed principle
concepts.statement: Modules should be open for extension and closed for modification.
concepts.notes: Assumes, untaught in the map: object-oriented programming.

concepts.name: Liskov substitution principle
concepts.statement: Objects of a subtype must be usable wherever the base type is expected without breaking correctness.
concepts.notes: Assumes, untaught in the map: object-oriented programming.

concepts.name: Interface segregation principle
concepts.statement: Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use.
concepts.notes: Assumes, untaught in the map: object-oriented programming.

concepts.name: Dependency inversion principle
concepts.statement: High-level modules should depend on abstractions, not on low-level modules.
concepts.notes: Assumes, untaught in the map: object-oriented programming.

concepts.name: OOD: design a parking lot
concepts.statement: Design a multi-level parking lot with motorcycle, compact and large spots, where a bus takes five consecutive large spots.

concepts.name: OOD: design a call center
concepts.statement: Design a call center where operators take calls first and escalate to supervisors, then directors, queueing calls when no one is free.

concepts.name: OOD: design a deck of cards
concepts.statement: Design a generic 52-card deck and extend it to blackjack.

concepts.name: OOD: design an online chat
concepts.statement: Design text chat with users, friend requests, private and group chats.

concepts.name: Using vi(m) and Emacs
concepts.statement: Edit code efficiently in a Unix editor: modes and motions in vim, buffers and commands in Emacs.

concepts.name: Unix command-line tools
concepts.statement: Use bash, cat, grep, sed, awk, curl/wget, sort, tr, uniq, strace and tcpdump.

concepts.name: Information theory
concepts.statement: Information measured in bits, as introduced by Shannon.
concepts.notes: Tier set to core in the spec (sources say ciu stretch): crypto-hash (core) rests on it.

concepts.name: Entropy
concepts.statement: The expected information of a source, H = -sum p log2 p bits per symbol, bounding lossless compression.

concepts.name: Parity bits
concepts.statement: An extra bit making the count of 1s even (or odd) detects any single-bit error.

concepts.name: Hamming code
concepts.statement: Parity bits at power-of-two positions locate, and so correct, any single-bit error.

concepts.name: Lossless compression
concepts.statement: Remove redundancy to store data in fewer bits, up to the limit set by entropy.

concepts.name: LZ77
concepts.statement: Replace repeated substrings with (distance, length) references back into a sliding window.

concepts.name: Cryptographic hash functions
concepts.statement: Hash functions that are infeasible to invert or to find collisions for.
concepts.notes: Tier set to core in the spec (sources say ciu stretch): shortlink-generation (core) rests on it.

concepts.name: Encryption
concepts.statement: Symmetric and public-key schemes keep messages secret given a key.

concepts.name: Threat models and privilege separation
concepts.statement: Security design starts from what an attacker can do; privilege separation, capabilities and sandboxing limit the damage of a compromise.

concepts.name: Control hijacking and buffer overflows
concepts.statement: Overflowing a buffer can overwrite a return address and divert control; defences include stack canaries, non-executable memory and ASLR.

concepts.name: Web security model
concepts.statement: Same-origin policy, and defending web applications against injection, XSS and CSRF.

concepts.name: Network security and side channels
concepts.statement: Attacks on network protocols, and leaks through timing and other side channels.

concepts.name: Four-step system design interview approach
concepts.statement: Lead the open-ended conversation in four steps: outline use cases, constraints and assumptions; sketch a high-level design of the main components and connections and justify it; dive into the core components; then identify and address bottlenecks, discussing trade-offs, since everything is a trade-off.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (sdp:interview-approach, ciu:sd-process). Tier set to core in the spec (sources say sdp core, ciu stretch): requirements-scoping, core-component-design and iterative-scaling (core) rest on it.

concepts.name: Scoping use cases, constraints and assumptions
concepts.statement: Ask who uses the system and how, how many users, what it does, its inputs and outputs, how much data, how many requests per second and the read:write ratio; then fix in-scope and out-of-scope use cases and state assumptions (e.g. traffic not evenly distributed).

concepts.name: Designing core components per use case
concepts.statement: For each use case, trace the data flow through named services (client, web server, API servers, services, stores), give table schemas with their indexes, a public REST API and internal RPC, and ask the interviewer how much code to write.

concepts.name: Iterative scaling loop
concepts.statement: Scale a design iteratively: benchmark or load test, profile for bottlenecks, address them while weighing alternatives and trade-offs, and repeat; don't jump from the initial design straight to the final one.

concepts.name: Latency numbers every programmer should know
concepts.statement: Reference costs: L1 reference 0.5 ns, main memory 100 ns, 1 KB over 1 Gbps 10 us, 4 KB random SSD read 150 us, 1 MB sequential from memory 250 us, datacenter round trip 500 us, 1 MB from SSD 1 ms, disk seek 10 ms, 1 MB from disk 30 ms, California-Netherlands round trip 150 ms; hence disk about 30 MB/s, 1 Gbps about 100 MB/s, SSD about 1 GB/s, memory about 4 GB/s, about 2,000 datacenter round trips per second.

concepts.name: Requests-per-month conversion
concepts.statement: A month has about 2.5 million seconds, so 1 request/s is about 2.5 million requests/month, 40 requests/s about 100 million and 400 requests/s about 1 billion.

concepts.name: Back-of-the-envelope estimation
concepts.statement: Turn stated assumptions into size per item, new storage per month and per 3 years, and average reads, writes and searches per second, then use those numbers to justify components (e.g. 4 writes/s fits one SQL master; 60,000 fan-out deliveries/s does not).
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (sdp:back-of-envelope, ciu:back-of-envelope). Tier set to core in the spec (sources say sdp core, ciu stretch): the core worked designs rest on it.

concepts.name: Performance vs scalability
concepts.statement: A service is scalable if its performance increases in proportion to resources added; with a performance problem the system is slow for a single user, with a scalability problem it is fast for one user but slow under heavy load.

concepts.name: Latency vs throughput
concepts.statement: Latency is the time to perform an action or produce a result; throughput is the number of such actions or results per unit time; aim for maximal throughput with acceptable latency.

concepts.name: Fallacies of distributed computing
concepts.statement: Networks are not reliable, latency is not zero, bandwidth is not infinite, and so on; designs must assume the opposite.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (ciu:distributed-fallacies, wp:Fallacies_of_distributed_computing). Open prose added in the gap inventory from dossiers/sweep-system-design.md §2.4.

concepts.name: CAP theorem
concepts.statement: A distributed system can support only two of consistency (every read receives the most recent write or an error), availability (every request receives a response, possibly not the latest) and partition tolerance (it keeps operating despite network partitions); networks are unreliable, so the real choice is between consistency and availability.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (sdp:cap-theorem, ciu:cap-theorem). Tier set to core in the spec (sources say sdp core, ciu stretch): weak, eventual and strong consistency (core) rest on it.

concepts.name: Weak consistency
concepts.statement: After a write, reads may or may not see it (best effort), as in memcached; suits realtime uses such as VoIP, video chat and multiplayer games.

concepts.name: Eventual consistency
concepts.statement: After a write, reads eventually see it (typically within milliseconds) because data is replicated asynchronously, as in DNS and email; suits highly available systems.

concepts.name: Strong consistency
concepts.statement: After a write, reads see it because data is replicated synchronously, as in file systems and RDBMSes; suits systems that need transactions.

concepts.name: CP vs AP systems
concepts.statement: A CP system waits for the partitioned node and may time out, a good choice when the business needs atomic reads and writes; an AP system answers with the most readily available, possibly stale, data and propagates writes once the partition heals, a good choice when eventual consistency is acceptable or the system must keep working despite external errors.

concepts.name: Consensus: Paxos and Raft
concepts.statement: Replicas can agree on a sequence of values despite failures of a minority, via Paxos or the more understandable Raft (leader election plus log replication).
concepts.notes: Merged 4 rows (ciu:consensus, raft-site:index.html, wp:Raft_(algorithm), wp:Paxos_(computer_science)). Open prose added in the gap inventory from dossiers/sweep-system-design.md §1, §2.1 and §2.4.

concepts.name: Active-passive fail-over
concepts.statement: Heartbeats run between an active server and a standby; if they stop, the passive server takes over the active's IP address. Downtime depends on hot or cold standby, and only the active server handles traffic (also called master-slave failover).

concepts.name: Active-active fail-over
concepts.statement: Both servers handle traffic and share the load; for public-facing servers DNS must know both public IPs, for internal ones application logic must know both (also called master-master failover).

concepts.name: Availability in nines
