concepts.statement: Availability is uptime as a percentage of time, counted in 9s: 99.9% allows about 8h 46m downtime a year (1m 26s a day), 99.99% about 52m 36s a year (8.6s a day).

concepts.name: Availability in sequence vs in parallel
concepts.statement: Components in sequence multiply availabilities, A = A_foo * A_bar (two 99.9% parts give 99.8%); components in parallel give A = 1 - (1 - A_foo)(1 - A_bar) (two 99.9% parts give 99.9999%).

concepts.name: Domain name system
concepts.statement: DNS translates a domain name to an IP address through a hierarchy of servers topped by a few authoritative ones; lower-level servers, the OS and the browser cache answers for a TTL, so mappings can go stale. Lookups add a small delay, management is complex, and DNS services can be taken down by DDoS.

concepts.name: DNS record types
concepts.statement: NS names the DNS servers for a domain, MX the mail servers, A points a name to an IP address, CNAME points a name to another name or to an A record.

concepts.name: DNS traffic routing
concepts.statement: Managed DNS such as Route 53 or CloudFlare can route by weighted round robin (keep traffic off servers in maintenance, balance unequal clusters, A/B test), by latency or by geolocation.

concepts.name: Content delivery network
concepts.statement: A CDN is a globally distributed network of proxy servers serving content, usually static files, from locations close to the user; users get faster responses and your servers skip the requests the CDN fulfils. Costs, content stale until its TTL expires, and URLs rewritten to point at the CDN are the drawbacks.

concepts.name: Push vs pull CDNs
concepts.statement: A push CDN receives content you upload whenever it changes, minimising traffic but maximising storage, and suits low-traffic or rarely updated sites; a pull CDN fetches content from your server on first request and caches it for a TTL, minimising storage but making the first request slow and possibly re-pulling unchanged files, and suits heavy traffic.

concepts.name: Load balancer
concepts.statement: A load balancer distributes client requests to application servers or databases and returns their responses, keeping requests off unhealthy servers, preventing overload and helping remove a single point of failure; it can also terminate SSL and keep session persistence. One load balancer is itself a single point of failure, so several run in active-passive or active-active mode, at the cost of complexity.

concepts.name: Load balancer routing methods
concepts.statement: Load balancers can route by random choice, least loaded, session or cookie, round robin or weighted round robin, or by layer 4 or layer 7 information.

concepts.name: Layer 4 vs layer 7 load balancing
concepts.statement: A layer 4 balancer looks only at transport-layer source and destination IPs and ports and forwards packets with NAT; a layer 7 balancer terminates the connection, reads headers, message and cookies, and routes by content (e.g. video traffic to video hosts, billing to hardened servers). Layer 4 needs less time and compute, layer 7 is more flexible.

concepts.name: Reverse proxy (web server)
concepts.statement: A reverse proxy is a web server that centralises internal services behind one public interface, forwarding each request to a server that can fulfil it and returning the response. It hides backends, can blacklist IPs and limit connections per client, lets you change servers behind one IP, terminates SSL, compresses and caches responses and serves static content; it adds complexity and is a single point of failure unless replicated.

concepts.name: Load balancer vs reverse proxy
concepts.statement: A load balancer is useful when several servers serve the same function; a reverse proxy is useful even with a single web or application server; NGINX and HAProxy can do both layer 7 proxying and load balancing.

concepts.name: Horizontal vs vertical scaling
concepts.statement: Scaling out on commodity machines behind load balancers is cheaper and more available than scaling up a single server on bigger hardware (vertical scaling), and easier to hire for; it costs complexity, cloned servers, and more simultaneous connections on downstream caches and databases.

concepts.name: Stateless web and application servers
concepts.statement: Servers that scale horizontally should be stateless: sessions and user data such as profile pictures live in a central database or persistent cache (Redis, Memcached), not on the server.

concepts.name: Scaling a web service: clones, databases, caches, asynchrony
concepts.statement: Stateless app servers behind load balancers, database replication and denormalisation, caching and queued background work are the standard scaling steps.
aliases: Scalable web architecture and distributed systems
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (ciu:scaling-basics, aosa:v2/distsys). Tier set to core in the spec (sources say ciu stretch, aosa core): sharding (core) rests on it. Open prose added in the gap inventory from dossiers/sweep-system-design.md §2.1.

concepts.name: Autoscaling
concepts.statement: Use autoscaling groups for web servers and each application server type across availability zones, with a min and max instance count, scaling on time of day for predictable load or on CPU, latency, network or custom metrics; it keeps up with spikes and powers down idle instances but adds complexity and lags demand.

concepts.name: Separating web and application layers
concepts.statement: Separating the web layer from the application (platform) layer lets each scale and be configured independently: a new API adds application servers without adding web servers. Small autonomous services follow the single responsibility principle, and application-layer workers enable asynchronism.

concepts.name: Microservices
concepts.statement: Microservices are a suite of independently deployable, small, modular services, each running its own process and communicating through a lightweight mechanism toward a business goal (e.g. Pinterest: user profile, follower, feed, search, photo upload); they add deployment and operational complexity.

concepts.name: Service discovery
concepts.statement: Systems such as Consul, Etcd and ZooKeeper let services find each other by tracking registered names, addresses and ports; health checks, often over HTTP, verify each service, and their built-in key-value store holds config and shared data.

concepts.name: Object store for blobs
concepts.statement: A managed object store such as Amazon S3 holds paste contents, media, static files and raw log files, while the SQL database keeps metadata and the object's path; it handles the designs' tens of GB to TB of new content per month.

concepts.name: Offloading static content to an object store and CDN
concepts.statement: Move static content (user files, JS, CSS, images, videos) to a managed object store, then serve it, and some dynamic content, from a CDN, reducing web server load and latency.

concepts.name: Monitoring and automated operations
concepts.statement: Automate DevOps (Chef, Puppet, Ansible) and keep monitoring at host level, aggregate level (load balancer stats), through log analysis, external site performance, incident notification and error reporting to catch new bottlenecks.
concepts.notes: Tier raised from stretch to core: it is a prerequisite of design-scaling-aws (core).

concepts.name: Security basics
concepts.statement: Encrypt in transit and at rest, sanitize all user inputs to prevent XSS and SQL injection, use parameterized queries, and apply the principle of least privilege.

concepts.name: Locking down hosts and network
concepts.statement: Open only necessary ports (80, 443, and 22 from whitelisted IPs), stop the web server initiating outbound connections, and put the web tier in a public subnet of a VPC with everything else in a private subnet, opening ports only to whitelisted IPs.
concepts.notes: Tier raised from stretch to core: it is a prerequisite of design-scaling-aws (core).

concepts.name: ACID transactions
concepts.statement: Relational database transactions are atomic (all or nothing), consistent (from one valid state to another), isolated (concurrent execution gives the same result as serial) and durable (committed stays committed).

concepts.name: Database normalisation
concepts.statement: 1NF to 4NF remove redundancy by splitting tables so every non-key fact depends on the key.

concepts.name: Database indices
concepts.statement: Indices on queried columns (SELECT, GROUP BY, ORDER BY, JOIN) speed queries; they are usually self-balancing B-trees giving logarithmic search, sequential access, insertion and deletion; they take memory and slow writes, and bulk loads can be faster with indices dropped then rebuilt.
concepts.notes: Edge to b-tree dropped: knowing an index is a B-tree is Essential; its operations are Advanced (user ruling 2026-11-08)

concepts.name: Tightening the schema
concepts.statement: Use CHAR for fixed-length fields (fast random access), TEXT for large text, INT for numbers up to 2^32, DECIMAL for currency, store the location of large BLOBs rather than the BLOBs, VARCHAR(255) as the largest length countable in one byte, and NOT NULL where possible.

concepts.name: Master-slave replication
concepts.statement: The master serves reads and writes and replicates writes to slaves that serve only reads, possibly in a tree; if the master goes offline the system runs read-only until a slave is promoted or a new master provisioned, which needs extra logic.

concepts.name: Master-master replication
concepts.statement: Both masters serve reads and writes and coordinate on writes, so writes continue if either fails; a load balancer or application logic must choose where to write, most such systems are either loosely consistent (violating ACID) or slower to write, and conflict resolution grows with more writers and latency.

concepts.name: Replication drawbacks and lag
concepts.statement: Data written to a master can be lost if it fails before replicating; replicas replaying many writes have less capacity for reads; more read slaves mean more replication lag; replicas may apply writes single-threaded; replication adds hardware and complexity.

concepts.name: Read replicas with read/write splitting
concepts.statement: Add read replicas to relieve the write master, put load balancers in front of them, and add logic so writes go to the master and reads to replicas; most services are read-heavy.

concepts.name: Federation (functional partitioning)
concepts.statement: Federation splits databases by function (e.g. forums, users, products): each sees less read and write traffic and replication lag, more of its data fits in memory for more cache hits, and writes proceed in parallel; but application logic must pick the database, cross-database joins need a server link, it fails for huge functions or tables, and it adds hardware.

concepts.name: Sharding
concepts.statement: Sharding distributes data across databases so each manages a subset (e.g. users by last-name initial or location): less traffic, replication and index size per shard, more cache hits, parallel writes, and a failed shard leaves the others up. Application logic and SQL get complex, power users can make a shard lopsided, rebalancing is costly (a consistent-hashing shard function reduces data moved), and cross-shard joins are hard.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (sdp:sharding, ciu:sharding). Tier set to core in the spec (sources say sdp core, ciu stretch): denormalization, cache-cluster-partitioning and several worked designs (core) rest on it.

concepts.name: Denormalization
concepts.statement: Denormalization writes redundant copies of data into several tables to avoid expensive joins, improving reads (which can outnumber writes 100:1 or 1000:1) at the cost of writes; materialized views can maintain the copies, and it avoids joins across federated or sharded data. Data is duplicated, constraints get complex, and under heavy writes it can perform worse.

concepts.name: SQL tuning
concepts.statement: Benchmark (e.g. with ab) and profile (e.g. the slow query log) to find bottlenecks, then tighten the schema, use good indices, avoid expensive joins by denormalizing, partition hot spots into separate tables, and tune the query cache.

concepts.name: Consistent hashing
concepts.statement: Place nodes and keys on a hash ring so adding or removing a node moves only about 1/n of the keys.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (ciu:consistent-hashing, wp:Consistent_hashing). Open prose added in the gap inventory from dossiers/sweep-system-design.md §1 and §2.4.

concepts.name: Distributed hash tables
concepts.statement: Spreading a key space across many machines by hashing keys to nodes, as in large storage systems.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (ciu:distributed-hash-table, wp:Distributed_hash_table). Open prose added in the gap inventory from dossiers/sweep-system-design.md §1 and §2.4.

concepts.name: Keeping hot data in the database, the rest in a warehouse
concepts.statement: Store only a limited recent window (e.g. a month of transactions) in the SQL database and the rest in a data warehouse (Redshift, BigQuery) or object store; keep analytics aggregates in a separate analytics database.
concepts.notes: Tier raised from stretch to core: it is a prerequisite of design-sales-rank (core).

concepts.name: NoSQL and BASE
concepts.statement: NoSQL stores (key-value, document, wide column, graph) keep data denormalized with joins done in application code, mostly lack true ACID transactions and favour eventual consistency; BASE (basically available, soft state, eventual consistency) chooses availability over consistency.

concepts.name: Key-value store
concepts.statement: A key-value store (abstraction: hash table) gives O(1) reads and writes, often backed by memory or SSD; some keep keys in lexicographic order for range retrieval. Its few operations push complexity into the application; it suits simple data models and fast-changing data such as an in-memory cache layer, and underlies document stores and some graph databases.

concepts.name: Document store
concepts.statement: A document store (abstraction: key-value store with documents as values) keeps all of an object's information in one XML, JSON or binary document and queries by the document's internal structure; documents grouped by collection, tag, metadata or directory can have entirely different fields. MongoDB, CouchDB, DynamoDB; flexible, for occasionally changing data.

concepts.name: Wide column store
concepts.statement: A wide column store (abstraction: ColumnFamily<RowKey, Columns<ColKey, Value, Timestamp>>) stores columns, name/value pairs with timestamps for versioning and conflict resolution, grouped into column families and accessed by row key; Bigtable, HBase and Cassandra keep keys ordered for range scans and give high availability and scalability for very large data sets.

concepts.name: Graph database
concepts.statement: In a graph database each node is a record and each arc a relationship; it is optimised for many foreign keys or many-to-many relationships such as social networks, but tooling is younger and many are reachable only through REST APIs.
concepts.notes: Tier raised from stretch to core: it is a prerequisite of sql-vs-nosql (core).

concepts.name: NoSQL patterns
concepts.statement: Key-value, column and document stores scale by partitioning, replication and relaxed consistency.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (ciu:nosql-patterns, aosa:v1/nosql). Open prose added in the gap inventory from dossiers/sweep-system-design.md §2.1.

concepts.name: SQL or NoSQL
concepts.statement: Choose SQL for structured, relational data with a strict schema, complex joins, transactions, clear scaling patterns and fast indexed lookups; choose NoSQL for semi-structured or non-relational data with a dynamic schema, many TB or PB, very data-intensive workloads or very high IOPS, e.g. clickstream and log ingest, leaderboards, shopping carts, hot tables, metadata and lookup tables.

concepts.name: Caching
concepts.statement: A cache returns a previously computed result instead of re-executing the request, improving page load times and reducing server and database load; in front of a database it absorbs the uneven load popular items cause and traffic spikes.

concepts.name: Where to cache
concepts.statement: Caches can sit on the client (OS or browser), in a CDN, at the web server or reverse proxy (e.g. Varnish), in the database's own cache (tune its defaults to the usage pattern), or in an application cache layer.

concepts.name: In-memory application cache
concepts.statement: In-memory caches such as Memcached and Redis are key-value stores between the application and data storage; RAM is fast but limited, so eviction such as least recently used keeps hot data. Redis adds persistence and data structures such as sorted sets and lists. Avoid file-based caching, which hinders cloning and autoscaling.

concepts.name: What to cache: query level vs object level
concepts.statement: Caching at the database query level stores results keyed by a hash of the query, but is hard to invalidate when any underlying cell changes; caching at the object level stores assembled objects, removed when their data changes, and lets workers build objects asynchronously. Good candidates: user sessions, fully rendered pages, activity streams, user graph data.

concepts.name: Redis as an in-memory data store
concepts.statement: An in-memory key-value store with rich data types, used as a cache and message broker.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (ciu:redis, wp:Redis). Open prose added in the gap inventory from dossiers/sweep-system-design.md §2.4.

concepts.name: Spreading a cache over many machines
concepts.statement: Each machine can keep its own cache (simple, low hit rate), a full copy (simple, wastes memory), or a shard chosen by machine = hash(query) (more complex, likely best), ideally with consistent hashing.

concepts.name: Cache-aside (lazy loading)
concepts.statement: The application looks up the cache; on a miss it loads the entry from the database, adds it to the cache and returns it; the cache never talks to storage. Only requested data is cached, but each miss costs three trips, entries go stale unless a TTL or write-through refreshes them, and a replacement node starts empty.

concepts.name: Write-through cache
concepts.statement: The application reads and writes the cache as its main store and the cache synchronously writes the database: writes are slow but freshly written data reads fast and is never stale; a new node caches nothing until entries are updated (pair with cache-aside), and much written data is never read (mitigate with a TTL).

concepts.name: Write-behind (write-back) cache
concepts.statement: The application writes the cache, which writes the data store asynchronously: writes get faster, but data is lost if the cache goes down before it reaches the store, and it is harder to implement than cache-aside or write-through.

concepts.name: Refresh-ahead cache
concepts.statement: The cache automatically refreshes recently accessed entries before they expire; this lowers latency only if it predicts which items will be needed, otherwise performance is worse than without it.

concepts.name: Cache invalidation and TTL
concepts.statement: A cache must stay consistent with the source of truth; deciding when to update or invalidate it is hard, a time to live (TTL) bounds staleness most simply, and adding Redis or Memcached requires application changes.

concepts.name: Asynchronous workflows
concepts.statement: Asynchronous workflows take expensive operations out of the request path and can do time-consuming work in advance (e.g. periodic aggregation); cheap calculations and realtime workflows are better done synchronously, since queues add delay and complexity.

concepts.name: Message queues
concepts.statement: A message queue receives, holds and delivers messages: the application publishes a job and tells the user its status, a worker picks it up, processes it and signals completion, so the user isn't blocked (a client may show the result early, as a tweet appears on your timeline before followers receive it). Redis can lose messages, RabbitMQ needs AMQP and self-managed nodes, Amazon SQS is hosted but can be slow and deliver twice.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (sdp:message-queue, ciu:message-queues). Tier set to core in the spec (sources say sdp core, ciu stretch): back-pressure, fanout-on-write and several worked designs (core) rest on it.

concepts.name: Task queues
concepts.statement: A task queue receives tasks with their data, runs them and delivers results; it can schedule computationally intensive background jobs (e.g. Celery).

concepts.name: Back pressure
concepts.statement: If a queue grows larger than memory, cache misses and disk reads slow everything; back pressure caps the queue size to keep throughput and response times good for queued jobs, and answers new work with server busy / HTTP 503 so clients retry later, perhaps with exponential backoff.

concepts.name: MapReduce aggregation over logs
concepts.statement: Batch-aggregate logs with MapReduce: the mapper parses each line and emits (key, value) pairs such as ((month, url), 1) or ((user, month, category), amount); the reducer sums values per key. Used for paste hit counts, URL de-duplication, monthly spending and sales counts.
concepts.notes: Assumes, untaught in the map: MapReduce. Tier raised from stretch to core: it is a prerequisite of design-pastebin (core).

concepts.name: Distributed sort as a second MapReduce step
concepts.statement: A second MapReduce step re-keys ((category, product), total) as ((category, total), product) so the shuffle/sort phase sorts across machines, giving per-category rankings ready for a sales_rank table.
concepts.notes: Tier raised from stretch to core: it is a prerequisite of design-sales-rank (core).

concepts.name: Base62 encoding
concepts.statement: Base62 encodes a number in [a-zA-Z0-9] by repeated modulo and division by 62, in O(k) for k digits; unlike Base64 it has no + or / so URLs need no escaping, and it is deterministic.

concepts.name: Short link generation by hashing
concepts.statement: Generate a short link by MD5-hashing the user's IP address plus a timestamp (or random data), Base62-encoding it and keeping the first 7 characters: 62^7 values cover 360 million links in 3 years. Check the database for a duplicate and regenerate if found; the shortlink is the primary key, which indexes it and enforces uniqueness.

concepts.name: Design Pastebin / Bit.ly
concepts.statement: Design a paste service: anonymous users submit text and get a random short link with optional expiry, read pastes by link, and the service keeps monthly hit analytics and deletes expired pastes, at 10M writes and 100M reads a month.

concepts.name: Fan-out on write to home timelines
concepts.statement: When a user posts, the tweet is stored in the user's own timeline in SQL, and a Fan Out Service looks up the followers through the User Graph Service and inserts the tweet id into each follower's home timeline kept in a memory cache (a Redis list of tweet_id, user_id, meta) - O(followers), 60,000 deliveries/s. It also indexes the tweet for search, stores media and sends notifications through a queue. Reading a home timeline is then an O(1) cache read plus multigets to tweet and user info services.

concepts.name: Skipping fan-out for highly followed users
concepts.statement: Fanning out a tweet from a user with millions of followers can take minutes and race with @replies (fix by reordering at serve time); instead, don't fan out tweets from highly followed users, fetch them by search and merge them into the home timeline at serve time.

concepts.name: Bounding the timeline cache
concepts.statement: Keep only several hundred tweets per home timeline and only users active in the past 30 days in the memory cache, rebuilding an inactive user's timeline from SQL via the user graph; keep only a month of tweets in the tweet info service and only active users in the user info service.
concepts.notes: Tier raised from stretch to core: it is a prerequisite of design-twitter (core).

concepts.name: Reverse (inverted) index
concepts.statement: A reverse index maps words to the pages containing them; the crawler queues a job per page for a Reverse Index Service, which at query time finds and ranks matching documents, while a Document Service returns static titles and snippets.
concepts.notes: Tier raised from stretch to core: it is a prerequisite of search-query-processing (core).

concepts.name: Search query processing and scatter-gather
concepts.statement: A search service parses the query (remove markup, break into terms, fix typos, normalise capitalisation, convert to boolean operations), scatter-gathers it to every server of a search cluster such as Lucene, then merges, ranks, sorts and returns results.
concepts.notes: Tier raised from stretch to core: it is a prerequisite of design-twitter (core).

concepts.name: Design the Twitter timeline and search
concepts.statement: Design posting tweets with fan-out to followers and notifications, user and home timelines, and keyword search, at 500M tweets a day, 250B reads and 10B searches a month.

concepts.name: Crawl loop over a prioritised link store
concepts.statement: Keep links_to_crawl ranked by site popularity (e.g. a Redis sorted set) and crawled_links with page signatures in a NoSQL store; loop: take the top link; if a page with a similar signature was crawled, lower the link's priority (avoiding cycles) and continue; else crawl it, queue reverse-index and document jobs, create its signature, and move it from links_to_crawl to crawled_links.

concepts.name: Duplicate URL and content detection
concepts.statement: Remove duplicate URLs with sort | uniq for small lists or, at a billion links, a MapReduce that keeps entries of frequency 1; detect duplicate content by generating page signatures and comparing them with a similarity measure such as the Jaccard index or cosine similarity.

concepts.name: Recrawl freshness policy
concepts.statement: Record when each page was last crawled, refresh every page after a default period (say a week) and popular or frequently changing pages sooner (mine the mean time between updates), and optionally honour robots.txt.
concepts.notes: Tier raised from stretch to core: it is a prerequisite of design-web-crawler (core).

concepts.name: Crawler throughput optimisations
concepts.statement: Shard and federate the reverse index and document services, keep a crawler-side DNS cache refreshed periodically, keep many connections open through a pool (or switch to UDP), and provision enough bandwidth.
concepts.notes: Tier raised from stretch to core: it is a prerequisite of design-web-crawler (core).

concepts.name: Design a web crawler
concepts.statement: Design a crawler for 1B links refreshed weekly that builds a reverse index and static titles and snippets, plus the search front end, without getting stuck in cycles, at 4B pages crawled and 100B searches a month.

concepts.name: Categorising transactions by seller
concepts.statement: Seed a seller-to-category dictionary with the most popular sellers (50,000 entries under 255 bytes is about 12 MB); for unseeded sellers use crowd-sourced user overrides, keeping the top override per seller in a heap for O(1) lookup.

concepts.name: Budget templates with stored overrides
concepts.statement: Allocate default category budgets from an income-tier template and store only the categories users override, instead of 100 million budget rows; compute monthly spending per category with SQL over the transactions table or MapReduce over raw transaction files, re-running when a category changes.

concepts.name: Design Mint.com
concepts.statement: Design a personal finance service: users link financial accounts, the service extracts and categorises transactions daily, analyses monthly spending by category, recommends budgets and notifies users near their budget, at 5B transactions a month, write-heavy 10:1.

concepts.name: BFS over a sharded graph with a lookup service
concepts.statement: When users don't fit on one machine, shard them across Person Servers and keep a Lookup Service mapping person id to server; the User Graph Service runs BFS, asking the lookup service which server holds each friend before fetching it.

concepts.name: Speeding up distributed BFS
concepts.statement: Cache person data and complete or partial BFS traversals in memory, or batch-compute them offline into NoSQL; batch friend lookups on the same Person Server and shard servers by location; run two BFS searches from source and destination and merge; start from people with many friends; cap search time or hops before asking the user.

concepts.name: Distributed graph algorithms
concepts.statement: Synchronous and asynchronous distributed algorithms for symmetry breaking, BFS trees and shortest-path spanning trees.

concepts.name: Design the data structures for a social network
concepts.statement: Design shortest-path friend search over 100M users with 50 friends each (5B edges) that don't fit on one machine, at 400 searches/s, without a graph database.

concepts.name: Design a key-value cache for search query results
concepts.statement: Design a cache for the most recent web search results (10B queries a month, 4,000 requests/s, limited memory): serve hits fast, fill on misses, expire and refresh, and spread the cache over many machines.

concepts.name: Design Amazon's sales rank by category
concepts.statement: Design hourly computation and serving of the past week's most popular products per category over 10M products, 1,000 categories and 1B transactions a month, with 100B reads a month.

concepts.name: Design a system that scales to millions of users on AWS
concepts.statement: Evolve a read/write web service from one box to 10M users (1B writes and 100B reads a month), stage by stage, adding components only as benchmarks and profiling show bottlenecks.

concepts.name: Range minimum query problem
concepts.statement: Answer queries min(A[L..R]) on an array, possibly with updates; it also underlies LCA.

concepts.name: Sparse table
concepts.statement: A table st[i][j] holding the answer for the range [j, j+2^i-1], built in O(N log N) from st[i][j] = f(st[i-1][j], st[i-1][j+2^(i-1)]); it serves range queries on an immutable array.

concepts.name: Sparse table range query by power-of-two decomposition
concepts.statement: Any range splits into at most ceil(log2 length) disjoint power-of-two blocks, so an associative query (e.g. sum) is answered in O(log N) by combining those blocks from largest to smallest.

concepts.name: O(1) range minimum with a sparse table
concepts.statement: For an idempotent operation such as min, a range [L,R] is covered by two overlapping blocks of length 2^k with k = floor(log2(R-L+1)), giving O(1) queries after O(N log N) preprocessing.

concepts.name: Structures for O(1) associative range queries
concepts.statement: The overlapping-block trick needs idempotence; disjoint sparse tables and sqrt trees answer any associative range query in O(1).

concepts.name: Fenwick tree
concepts.statement: An array T where T[i] stores f over A[g(i)..i], g(i) clearing the trailing 1 bits of i (0-based; i & (i+1)); prefix queries follow i -> g(i)-1 and updates follow i -> i | (i+1), each O(log N), for a group operation f.

concepts.name: Fenwick tree for point update, range sum
concepts.statement: Implement sum(r) and add(i, delta) and answer [l,r] as sum(r) - sum(l-1); one-based variant uses i & -i (toggle the last set bit).

concepts.name: Linear-time Fenwick construction
concepts.statement: Build in O(N) by adding a[i] into T[i] and pushing T[i] once to its parent range i | (i+1).

concepts.name: Fenwick tree for prefix minimum
concepts.statement: With min (not a group) a Fenwick tree can answer only prefix-minimum queries and only under decreasing updates.

concepts.name: Fenwick range update with point / range query
concepts.statement: Range add [l,r] by x becomes add(l,x), add(r+1,-x) on a difference array, so a prefix sum gives a point value; two BITs B1, B2 with sum(B1,i)*i - sum(B2,i) give range-update range-query.

concepts.name: Segment tree
concepts.statement: A binary tree over array segments, each node storing the merge of its two halves (e.g. a sum), stored implicitly in an array with children 2v and 2v+1 in at most 4n cells.

concepts.name: Segment tree range query and point update
concepts.statement: A range query visits O(log n) nodes (fully-inside nodes return stored values, disjoint ones contribute nothing); a point update changes one node per level, also O(log n).

concepts.name: Segment tree with custom node values
concepts.statement: Change what a node stores and how children merge: maximum, maximum with count, gcd/lcm, or the four values (sum, best prefix, best suffix, best) for maximum subsegment sum.

concepts.name: Searching by descending the segment tree
concepts.statement: Find the k-th zero, the first prefix reaching a sum, or the first element above x in a range in O(log n) by walking down using child aggregates, instead of O(log^2 n) binary search over queries.

concepts.name: Lazy propagation
concepts.statement: For range updates, store a pending update at fully covered nodes and push it to the children only when a later operation descends there, keeping range add/assign with range queries at O(log n).

concepts.name: Merge sort tree
concepts.statement: Store each node's segment sorted (built by merging children); a lower-bound query over a range takes O(log^2 n), with multisets for updates and O(log n) with fractional cascading.

concepts.name: 2D segment tree
concepts.statement: A segment tree over rows whose nodes are segment trees over columns answers submatrix queries in O(log n log m); for sparse points the inner trees are built only over the points in each node.

concepts.name: Persistent segment tree
concepts.statement: An update copies only the O(log n) nodes on its path, keeping every past version; with versions over prefixes of values, the k-th smallest in a range is found in O(log n).

concepts.name: Dynamic (implicit) segment tree
concepts.statement: Create nodes lazily on first access so a tree over a huge index range uses memory proportional to the operations performed.

concepts.name: LIS with a prefix-maximum structure
concepts.statement: Process values in order and compute d[i] as one plus a prefix maximum over smaller values held in a segment or Fenwick tree (after coordinate compression); extends to counting LIS.

concepts.name: Sqrt decomposition for range queries
concepts.statement: Split the array into ~sqrt(n) blocks with precomputed block aggregates; a query sums two partial tails and whole blocks in O(sqrt n), and the scheme extends to range updates with per-block lazy values.
concepts.notes: Tier raised from contest to stretch: it is a prerequisite of rmq-approaches (stretch).

concepts.name: Mo's algorithm
concepts.statement: Answer offline range queries by sorting them by (block of left end, right end) and moving a window with add/remove; total O((N+Q) F sqrt N) for add/remove cost F.

concepts.name: Sqrt tree
concepts.statement: Recursively apply sqrt decomposition (prefixOp, suffixOp, between) to get a tree of height O(log log n); with power-of-two block sizes, any associative range query is O(1) after O(n log log n) preprocessing.

concepts.name: Sqrt tree updates
concepts.statement: Point updates in O(sqrt n) by indexing the root's between array with a nested sqrt tree; segment assignment with lazy marks in O(sqrt n log log n) or O(sqrt n) depending on which layers may be lazy.

concepts.name: Choosing an RMQ structure
concepts.statement: With updates: sqrt decomposition O(sqrt n) or segment tree O(log n); static: sparse table O(1) after O(n log n), sqrt tree, disjoint sparse table, Farach-Colton-Bender O(1) after O(n), or offline DSU / Arpa.

concepts.name: Painting subarrays offline with DSU
concepts.statement: Process repaint queries in reverse, with each cell's DSU parent pointing to the next unpainted cell, so every cell is painted exactly once and skipped thereafter.

concepts.name: DSU with distance/parity to the representative
concepts.statement: Store each node's distance (or parity) to its parent and fix it up during path compression; with parity this checks online whether components stay bipartite as edges are added.

concepts.name: Arpa's trick: offline RMQ with DSU
concepts.statement: Sweeping right, link each element to the next smaller element to its right via DSU; the answer to query (L,R) with R = current index is a[find_set(L)], giving O(alpha(n)) per query offline.

concepts.name: Small-to-large merging
concepts.statement: Always merge the smaller collection into the larger: each element moves O(log n) times, so explicit-list DSU costs O(m + n log n), and the same idea merges per-subtree sets in O(n log^2 n).

concepts.name: Undoing operations with a change stack (rollback DSU)
concepts.statement: A structure whose updates are worst-case O(T(n)) can be rolled back in O(T(n)) by pushing each modified cell's old value on a stack; DSU with union by rank but no path compression supports this, giving offline dynamic connectivity. Rollbacks break amortised bounds.

concepts.name: Offline deletion via segment tree over time
concepts.statement: Give each element its lifetime interval over the query sequence, insert it into the O(log n) segment-tree nodes covering that interval, and DFS the tree with rollback, so a structure with add in O(T(n)) supports deletion in O(T(n) log n) offline.

concepts.name: MEX of a sequence
concepts.statement: mex(A) is the smallest non-negative integer not in A; for |A| = N it is at most N.

concepts.name: Computing MEX in O(N)
concepts.statement: Mark values below N in a boolean array (ignoring larger ones) and scan for the first unmarked index.

concepts.name: MEX under point updates
concepts.statement: Keep counts of values 0..N in a segment tree (or a set of missing values) and descend to the first zero count, giving O(log N) per update.

concepts.name: Lowest common ancestor
concepts.statement: For vertices u, v of a rooted tree, the deepest vertex that is an ancestor of both (a vertex counts as its own ancestor).

concepts.name: LCA via Euler tour and range minimum
concepts.statement: Record the DFS Euler tour (2n-1 entries) with depths and each vertex's first occurrence; LCA(u, v) is the minimum-depth vertex between first[u] and first[v], so LCA reduces to RMQ (segment tree: O(log N) per query; sqrt decomposition: O(sqrt N)).

concepts.name: Binary lifting for LCA
concepts.statement: Precompute up[v][j], the 2^j-th ancestor, by DFS in O(N log N); with entry/exit times, lift u by decreasing powers while the ancestor is not an ancestor of v, answering LCA in O(log N).

concepts.name: Binary lifting with depths (supports adding leaves)
concepts.statement: Equalise depths by lifting the deeper vertex depth[u]-depth[v] steps, then lift both while their ancestors differ; new leaves only need their own up[] row.

concepts.name: LCA with O(n) space jump pointers
concepts.statement: Each vertex keeps its parent and one 'big' jump defined recursively from its parent's jumps (skew-binary); level ancestor and LCA queries run in O(log n) with O(n) space and preprocessing.

concepts.name: Farach-Colton and Bender LCA
concepts.statement: On the Euler tour depths (adjacent values differ by 1), split into blocks of size 0.5 log N; a sparse table over block minima plus precomputed answers for each of the O(sqrt N) possible +-1 block shapes give O(N) preprocessing and O(1) queries.

concepts.name: Static RMQ in O(N)/O(1) via Cartesian tree
concepts.statement: Build the min-Cartesian tree of the array with a stack in O(N); RMQ(L, R) is the LCA of L and R, answered in O(1) by Farach-Colton and Bender.

concepts.name: Tarjan's offline LCA
concepts.statement: One DFS with DSU: after finishing a child, union it into the current vertex and set the set's ancestor to the current vertex; a query (u, v) answered at u when v is visited is ancestor[find(v)]; O(n + m) total with DSU in alpha.

concepts.name: Heavy-light decomposition
concepts.statement: Mark the edge to a child with subtree at least half (or the largest) as heavy; heavy edges form disjoint paths and any root path crosses O(log n) light edges, so path queries split into O(log n) path segments.

concepts.name: Path queries with HLD and segment trees
concepts.statement: Lay heavy paths contiguously in one segment tree; max/sum queries and repainting on the path a-b take O(log^2 n) by walking both ends up chain by chain.

concepts.name: Centroid of a tree
concepts.statement: A vertex whose removal leaves no component with more than n/2 vertices; every tree has one or two, and two centroids are adjacent.

concepts.name: Centroid decomposition
concepts.statement: Recursively remove a centroid and decompose the remaining components; the recursion depth is O(log N) and every path passes through the centroid of some component, so path-counting problems run in O(N log N) times per-level work.

concepts.name: Counting painted edges on tree paths with Euler tour
concepts.statement: Split a path at the LCA into two ancestor-descendant paths; over the Euler tour keep segment trees of forward and backward edge colours, so the count on an ancestor path is T1[p..q-1] - T2[p..q-1], O(log N) per query and paint.

concepts.name: Prufer code
concepts.statement: Encode a labelled tree on n vertices as n-2 numbers by repeatedly removing the smallest-numbered leaf and writing down its neighbour; each vertex appears degree-1 times.

concepts.name: Prufer code and tree restoration in linear time
concepts.statement: A moving pointer to the smallest leaf works because only the just-reduced neighbour can become a new smaller leaf; the same trick rebuilds the tree from the code via the degrees, both O(n) (O(n log n) with a heap).

concepts.name: Cayley's formula
concepts.statement: Prufer codes biject labelled trees with sequences of n-2 values in [0, n-1], so the complete graph K_n has n^(n-2) spanning trees.

concepts.name: Ways to make a graph connected
concepts.statement: A graph with k components of sizes s1..sk can be made connected by adding k-1 edges in s1 s2 ... sk n^(k-2) ways (via Prufer codes and the multinomial theorem).
concepts.notes: Assumes, untaught in the map: multinomial theorem.

concepts.name: Flow networks and (s,t)-flows
concepts.statement: Given a directed graph with source s, target t and edge capacities c, a feasible (s,t)-flow assigns 0 <= f(e) <= c(e) to each edge with conservation at every vertex other than s and t; its value is the net flow out of s.
aliases: Flow network, flow and residual network
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (jeffe:flow, cpa:flow-network).

concepts.name: (s,t)-cuts and capacity
concepts.statement: An (s,t)-cut partitions V into S containing s and T containing t; its capacity is the total capacity of edges from S to T, and every flow's value is at most every cut's capacity.

concepts.name: Residual graphs and augmenting paths
concepts.statement: The residual graph of flow f has an edge u->v of capacity c(u->v)-f(u->v) and a reverse edge v->u of capacity f(u->v); an s-to-t path in it can push more flow.

concepts.name: Maxflow-mincut theorem
concepts.statement: In every flow network the maximum (s,t)-flow value equals the minimum (s,t)-cut capacity; a flow is maximum iff its residual graph has no s-to-t path.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (jeffe:maxflow-mincut, cpa:max-flow-min-cut). Edge to ford-fulkerson dropped: cpa proves the theorem through Ford-Fulkerson; Erickson states it first and derives the algorithm from it. Breaks a cycle.

concepts.name: Combining and decomposing flows
concepts.statement: Every acyclic (s,t)-flow is a sum of at most E path flows, and every flow is a sum of path flows and cycle flows, computable in O(VE) time.

concepts.name: Ford-Fulkerson augmenting paths
concepts.statement: Repeatedly augment along any residual s-to-t path; with integer capacities it terminates after at most |f*| augmentations in O(E|f*|) time with an integral maximum flow (integrality theorem); with irrational capacities it may not terminate.
concepts.notes: Merged 3 rows (jeffe:ford-fulkerson, cpa:ford-fulkerson, ciu:max-flow).

concepts.name: Integral flow theorem
concepts.statement: If all capacities are integers there is a maximum flow with integer flow on every edge (and Ford-Fulkerson finds one).

concepts.name: Edmonds-Karp augmenting-path rules
concepts.statement: Augmenting along the fattest path gives O(E log|f*|) augmentations; along the shortest (BFS) path gives O(VE) augmentations, i.e. O(VE^2) time independent of capacities.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (jeffe:edmonds-karp, cpa:edmonds-karp).

concepts.name: Dinic's algorithm
concepts.statement: In phases, build the BFS level graph of the residual network and find a blocking flow by DFS with per-vertex edge pointers; fewer than V phases as dist(s,t) strictly grows, giving O(V^2 E).

concepts.name: Dinic on unit networks
concepts.statement: On unit networks (each inner vertex has a single in- or out-edge, unit capacities) Dinic runs in O(E sqrt V); on general unit-capacity networks phases are O(sqrt E) and O(V^(2/3)).

concepts.name: MPM maximum flow
concepts.statement: Like Dinic but finds each blocking flow by repeatedly saturating the vertex of minimum potential min(in-capacity, out-capacity) in the layered network, giving O(V^3).

concepts.name: Preflow, excess and valid labeling
concepts.statement: A preflow obeys capacities but lets inflow exceed outflow (excess x(u) > 0 marks an active vertex); a valid labeling h has h(s) = |V|, h(t) = 0 and h(u) <= h(v) + 1 for every residual edge (u, v).

concepts.name: Push-relabel maximum flow
concepts.statement: Start with a preflow saturating source edges and heights h(s)=|V|; push excess along admissible residual edges (h(u) = h(v)+1) and relabel when none exists; O(V^2) relabels and O(VE) saturating pushes give O(V^2 E) with a FIFO of active vertices.

concepts.name: Highest-label push-relabel
concepts.statement: Always discharging an active vertex of greatest height reduces the bound to O(VE + V^2 sqrt E), i.e. O(V^3) worst case.

concepts.name: Faster maximum-flow algorithms (survey)
concepts.statement: Later algorithms (Dinitz's blocking flows, push-relabel, Orlin's O(VE)) improve on Edmonds-Karp; the section surveys them without proofs.

concepts.name: Matching, maximal and maximum matching, augmenting path
concepts.statement: A matching is a set of pairwise non-adjacent edges; maximal means no edge can be added, maximum means largest cardinality; an augmenting path alternates non-matching/matching edges between two unsaturated vertices.

concepts.name: Berge's lemma
concepts.statement: A matching is maximum iff no augmenting path exists relative to it; flipping an augmenting path increases the matching by one.

concepts.name: Kuhn's algorithm for maximum bipartite matching
concepts.statement: For each left vertex, search by DFS (try_kuhn) for an augmenting path and flip it; O(n1 m), so put the smaller part on the left; a greedy initial matching speeds it up.

concepts.name: Bipartite matching via maximum flow
concepts.statement: Add a source to all left vertices and a sink from all right vertices with unit capacities; integral maximum flows correspond to maximum matchings, found in O(VE) time.

concepts.name: Edge-disjoint paths
concepts.statement: The maximum number of edge-disjoint s-to-t paths equals the maximum flow with unit capacities (and the minimum number of edges whose removal separates s from t, Menger).

concepts.name: Vertex capacities and vertex-disjoint paths
concepts.statement: Split each vertex v into v_in -> v_out with capacity c(v) to reduce vertex-capacitated flow (and vertex-disjoint paths) to ordinary maximum flow.

concepts.name: Tuple selection (exam scheduling)
concepts.statement: Problems that select d-tuples with one element from each of several sets under per-element and per-pair capacities reduce to maximum flow through layered vertices, e.g. scheduling exams into rooms and times with proctors.

concepts.name: Disjoint-path covers of dags
concepts.statement: The minimum number of vertex-disjoint paths covering a dag equals V minus the size of a maximum matching in the bipartite split graph; with 'Minimal Faculty Hiring' as an application.

concepts.name: Baseball elimination
concepts.statement: A team is eliminated iff a flow network with game nodes and team nodes (capacities from remaining games and win slack) has no flow saturating all game edges; the min cut gives a certificate.

concepts.name: Project selection by minimum cut
concepts.statement: Choosing a dependency-closed set of projects maximizing total profit reduces to a minimum (s,t)-cut with profitable projects attached to s, costly ones to t, and infinite-capacity dependency edges.

concepts.name: Unbalanced flows: supplies and demands
concepts.statement: Generalize flows by giving each vertex a balance (supply or demand) and edges lower and upper bounds; feasibility reduces to one maximum flow from a super-source to a super-sink.

concepts.name: Pseudoflows and augmenting between imbalances
concepts.statement: A pseudoflow respects capacities but not conservation; repeatedly pushing flow along residual paths from excess to deficit vertices yields a feasible flow if one exists.

concepts.name: Flows with lower bounds (demands)
concepts.statement: Edges with demand d(e) <= f(e) <= c(e): add s', t', edges s'->v and v->t' carrying the demands, capacities c - d and an infinite t->s edge; a feasible flow exists iff the max s'-t' flow saturates all new edges; binary search on the t->s capacity gives the minimal flow.

concepts.name: Minimal flow with demands by binary search
concepts.statement: The infinite t->s edge carries the original network's flow; binary searching its capacity for the smallest value that still saturates the new edges gives the minimum feasible flow.

concepts.name: Minimum-cost circulations and cycle canceling
concepts.statement: A circulation is minimum-cost iff its residual graph has no negative-cost cycle; repeatedly canceling negative cycles (found by Bellman-Ford) terminates with an optimal integral circulation.

concepts.name: Minimum-cost flow by successive shortest paths
concepts.statement: Repeatedly augment along a cheapest s-t path in the residual network (reverse edges cost -c) until the required flow K is sent; O(F nm) with Bellman-Ford/SPFA, faster with Dijkstra and Johnson potentials.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (cpa:min-cost-flow, jeffe-notes:successive-shortest-paths).

concepts.name: Node potentials and reduced costs
concepts.statement: With potentials pi equal to shortest-path distances, the reduced costs c(u->v) + pi(u) - pi(v) are non-negative, so each successive-shortest-path step can use Dijkstra.

concepts.name: Assignment problem
concepts.statement: Given an n x n cost matrix, choose one entry in each row and column (a permutation) minimising the total; equivalently a minimum-weight perfect matching in a complete bipartite graph.

concepts.name: Hungarian algorithm
concepts.statement: Maintain potentials u, v with u[i] + v[j] <= A[i][j] (a lower bound by duality) and grow the matching along tight edges, adjusting potentials when stuck; adding rows one at a time with per-column minima gives O(n^2 m) (O(n^3)).

concepts.name: Assignment problem via min-cost flow
concepts.statement: Build source -> N workers -> N jobs -> sink with unit capacities and assignment costs on middle edges; a min-cost maximum flow of value N is an optimal assignment.

concepts.name: 2-CNF and the implication graph
concepts.statement: In 2-SAT every clause has two literals; each clause (a or b) is equivalent to not a -> b and not b -> a, giving a directed graph on 2n literal vertices.
concepts.notes: Assumes, untaught in the map: Boolean formula in CNF.

concepts.name: 2-SAT
concepts.statement: Turn each clause (a or b) into implications not a -> b and not b -> a; the formula is satisfiable iff no variable shares an SCC with its negation, and setting x true iff comp[x] comes after comp[not x] in topological order gives an assignment; O(n + m).

concepts.name: Online bridge finding with 2-edge-connected components
concepts.statement: Maintain the forest of 2-edge-connected components with two DSUs (components and 2ECCs) plus explicit parent pointers; a new edge either joins trees (re-rooting the smaller) or compresses the tree path between its ends into one 2ECC, in O(n log n + m) (the article's simplified DSU gives O(n log n + m log n)).

concepts.name: Strong orientation
concepts.statement: An undirected connected graph can be oriented to be strongly connected iff it has no bridges (Robbins); orienting tree edges down and back edges up in a DFS does it, and minimising SCCs in general takes components + bridges.

concepts.name: Edge and vertex connectivity
concepts.statement: Edge connectivity lambda (vertex connectivity kappa) is the fewest edges (vertices) whose removal disconnects the graph; it equals the minimum over pairs s, t of an s-t separating set's size.

concepts.name: Whitney inequalities
concepts.statement: kappa <= lambda <= delta, where delta is the minimum degree, and these cannot be improved in general.

concepts.name: Computing connectivity with max flow
concepts.statement: By Menger/Ford-Fulkerson, the max number of edge-disjoint s-t paths is a unit-capacity max flow; minimise over pairs (or use Stoer-Wagner); for vertex connectivity split each vertex into in/out with capacity 1.

concepts.name: Global minimum cut and edge contraction
concepts.statement: A minimum cut of a connected multigraph is a smallest set of edges whose removal disconnects it; contracting an edge merges its endpoints, keeps parallel edges and never decreases the minimum cut.
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (jeffe-notes:global-min-cut, cpa:global-min-cut). Source tiers differ (jeffe-notes stretch, cpa contest); reconciled to the most common, stretch.

concepts.name: Stoer-Wagner global minimum cut
concepts.statement: In each of n-1 phases grow a set A by the most tightly connected vertex; the last two added vertices s, t have min s-t cut equal to the weight of t's edges into A (Stoer-Wagner theorem); record it and merge s and t; O(n^3) simply, O(nm + n^2 log n) with a heap.

concepts.name: Karger's contraction algorithm
concepts.statement: Contracting uniformly random edges until two vertices remain returns a particular minimum cut with probability at least 2/(n(n-1)); repeating O(n^2 log n) times finds a minimum cut with high probability.

concepts.name: Karger-Stein recursive contraction
concepts.statement: Contract to about n/sqrt(2) vertices twice independently and recurse on each; success probability is Omega(1/log n) and the running time is O(n^2 log n), so O(n^2 log^3 n) gives high probability.

concepts.name: Second-best MST is one edge swap from the MST
concepts.statement: Some second-best spanning tree differs from a given MST by exactly one edge replacement, so it suffices to try removing one tree edge or adding one non-tree edge.

concepts.name: Second-best minimum spanning tree
concepts.statement: The second-best MST differs from the MST by one edge swap; adding each non-tree edge (u, v) and removing the heaviest tree edge on the u-v path (found with binary lifting / LCA) gives it in O(m log n).

concepts.name: LCP array (Kasai)
concepts.statement: The LCP of adjacent sorted suffixes is computed in O(n) because the LCP drops by at most one moving from suffix i to suffix i+1; the LCP of any two suffixes is then a range minimum.

concepts.name: Distinct substrings from suffix array and LCP
concepts.statement: The number of distinct substrings is sum over sorted suffixes of (n - p[i]) - lcp[i-1].

concepts.name: Aho-Corasick automaton
concepts.statement: Turn a trie into a DFA with suffix links (to the longest proper suffix that is a trie vertex) and transitions computed lazily or by BFS in O(mk); for one pattern this is KMP.

concepts.name: Multi-pattern search with Aho-Corasick
concepts.statement: Feed the text through the automaton and report matches via output (dictionary-suffix) links, in O(len + number of matches).

concepts.name: Search and DP over the Aho-Corasick automaton
concepts.statement: Problems on strings avoiding or containing dictionary words become paths in the automaton: avoid output states for the smallest non-matching string, BFS over (state, mask) for the shortest superstring, DFS over (state, length, count).

concepts.name: Suffix tree (Ukkonen's algorithm)
concepts.statement: Ukkonen's algorithm builds a suffix tree of s in O(n log k) for alphabet size k; code only.

concepts.name: Suffix automaton
concepts.statement: The minimal DFA accepting all suffixes of s; every path from the initial state spells a substring of s and every substring is one such path.
concepts.notes: Assumes, untaught in the map: finite automaton.

concepts.name: endpos classes and suffix links
concepts.statement: States correspond to classes of substrings with equal end-position sets; each class holds suffixes of its longest member of consecutive lengths, and the suffix link points to the class of the next shorter suffix, forming a tree.

concepts.name: Online linear-time suffix automaton construction
concepts.statement: Add characters one at a time, creating a state, walking suffix links to add transitions, and cloning a state when a transition is non-continuous; total time O(n log k) with map transitions, O(n) for constant alphabet.

concepts.name: Suffix automaton size bounds
concepts.statement: A suffix automaton of a length-n string has at most 2n-1 states (n >= 2) and at most 3n-4 transitions (n >= 3).

concepts.name: Suffix automaton applications
concepts.statement: Occurrence checks, counting distinct substrings and their total length (DP over the DAG), k-th substring, occurrence counts and positions, shortest absent string and longest common substring of two or many strings.

concepts.name: Palindrome radii d_odd and d_even
concepts.statement: All palindromic substrings are described compactly by, for each center, the number of palindromes centered there (d_odd[i], d_even[i]), since palindromes with a common center are nested.

concepts.name: Manacher's algorithm
concepts.statement: Keep the rightmost found palindrome (l, r); for i inside it start from the mirror's value min(r - i, d[l + r - i]) and extend naively; every extension moves r right, so all radii take O(n).

concepts.name: Manacher with interleaved separators
concepts.statement: Insert # between characters so even palindromes become odd ones; d[2i] and d[2i+1] recover d_even and d_odd from one odd-only pass.

concepts.name: Repetitions (squares) in a string
concepts.statement: A repetition is a substring of the form tt; a string can contain O(n^2) of them, but they group into O(n) runs described by 4-tuples.

concepts.name: Main-Lorentz algorithm
concepts.statement: Divide and conquer: recurse on halves, then find repetitions crossing the middle as tuples using Z-functions of the halves and reversed halves (left and right crossing criteria), in O(n log n) overall.

concepts.name: Lyndon word and Lyndon factorization
concepts.statement: A string is simple (Lyndon) if it is strictly smaller than all its proper suffixes (equivalently, all its nontrivial cyclic shifts); every string factors uniquely as w1 w2 ... wk of simple strings with w1 >= w2 >= ... >= wk.

concepts.name: Duval's algorithm
concepts.statement: A greedy scan over s = s1 s2 s3 (s2 pre-simple) emits the Lyndon factorization in O(n) time and O(1) extra memory.

concepts.name: Smallest cyclic shift
concepts.statement: The lexicographically least rotation starts at the last Lyndon factor of s + s that begins in the first half, found in O(n) by Duval; the suffix array and suffix automaton give alternatives.

concepts.name: Monotone optimal split point
concepts.statement: opt(i, j), the smallest k minimising the transition for dp(i, j), is monotone: opt(i, j) <= opt(i, j+1); this is the precondition that divide-and-conquer DP relies on.

concepts.name: Divide and conquer DP optimization
concepts.statement: For dp(i,j) = min_k dp(i-1,k-1) + C(k,j) with monotone optimal split opt(i,j) in j, compute a row by solving the middle j and recursing with narrowed k ranges, in O(n log n) per row instead of O(n^2).

concepts.name: Quadrangle inequality
concepts.statement: C(a,c) + C(b,d) <= C(a,d) + C(b,c) for a <= b <= c <= d; with monotonicity it implies monotone optimal splits, the precondition for D&C and Knuth optimizations.

concepts.name: Knuth's optimization
concepts.statement: For range DP dp(i,j) = min over i<=k<j of dp(i,k) + dp(k+1,j) + C(i,j), if C satisfies the quadrangle inequality and monotonicity then opt(i,j-1) <= opt(i,j) <= opt(i+1,j), so restricting k reduces O(n^3) to O(n^2).
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (cpa:knuth-optimization, jeffe-notes:knuth-monotonicity).

concepts.name: Total monotonicity and the SMAWK algorithm
concepts.statement: In a totally monotone matrix the row minima can be found in O(m + n) time by SMAWK (reduce columns, recurse on even rows, interpolate odd rows), which speeds up many DPs.

concepts.name: Saving space by divide and conquer (Hirschberg)
concepts.statement: An optimal edit-distance alignment can be recovered in O(mn) time and O(m + n) space by finding where the optimal path crosses the middle row and recursing on both halves.

concepts.name: Saving time with sparseness
concepts.statement: When few table entries matter (e.g. few matching character pairs in LCS), the DP can be computed from those key entries only, in time near-linear in their number.
concepts.notes: Edge to longest-common-subsequence added: Hunt-Szymanski's sparse DP is stated on LCS.

concepts.name: The Four Russians speedup
concepts.statement: Precomputing all small t x t blocks of a DP table with tiny alphabets, for t = Theta(log n), cuts the work by a factor of about log^2 n (e.g. edit distance in O(n^2 / log n)).

concepts.name: DP on broken profile
concepts.statement: Tile a grid row by row with state (row, bitmask of cells already filled in the next row) to count or optimise domino-type fillings, e.g. the 'Parquet' problem.

concepts.name: Non-attacking bishops by diagonal DP
concepts.statement: Black and white diagonals are independent; sorting diagonals of one colour by length, D[i][j] = D[i-1][j] + D[i-1][j-1](d_i - j + 1), and the answer convolves the two colours.

concepts.name: DFA minimization by dynamic programming
concepts.statement: Two DFA states are distinguishable iff some string leads one to accept and the other to reject; filling the distinguishability table by string length computes the minimal DFA in polynomial time.
concepts.notes: Assumes, untaught in the map: DFA.

concepts.name: NFA acceptance and regular-expression matching
concepts.statement: Whether an NFA (or a regular expression, via an equivalent NFA or a direct recurrence on subexpressions) accepts a string of length n is decided by DP over (position, state) in polynomial time.

concepts.name: Context-free parsing (CYK)
concepts.statement: For a grammar in Chomsky normal form, whether a nonterminal derives each substring is computed by DP over substring intervals in O(n^3) time.

concepts.name: Bloom filters
concepts.statement: Represent a set by an m-bit array and k hash functions, setting bits h_1(x)..h_k(x) on insertion; queries never give false negatives and the false-positive rate is about (1 - e^{-kn/m})^k, minimized near k = (m/n) ln 2.

concepts.name: The streaming model
concepts.statement: A streaming algorithm reads a long sequence once and must answer queries about it using space much smaller than the stream.

concepts.name: Count-min sketch
concepts.statement: Keep d rows of w counters with independent hash functions; estimating a frequency as the minimum of its d counters never underestimates and overestimates by more than eps*N with probability at most delta when w = e/eps and d = ln(1/delta).
concepts.notes: Merged 2 rows (jeffe-notes:count-min-sketch, wp:Count–min_sketch). Open prose added in the gap inventory from dossiers/sweep-system-design.md §2.4.

concepts.name: HyperLogLog
concepts.statement: Estimate the number of distinct items in a stream from the maximum run of leading zeros in their hashes, using kilobytes of memory.
